#8853. Are High-Intensity Workouts Messing With Your Cortisol?

If you’ve scrolled through social media lately, you’ve probably seen wellness influencers claim high-intensity exercise increases cortisol, the infamous “stress hormone” that, in excess amounts, can lead to fatigue, weight gain, trouble sleeping, high blood pressure, and elevated blood sugar.

Many influencers say to switch to a no-stress, low-sweat regimen. And while low-intensity exercises such as Pilates, treadmill walking, or yoga are valid ways to work out—and serve as excellent cross-training activities for runners—HIIT workouts (like hill repeats, sprint intervals, and tempo runs) are key if you’re training for a race or looking to build speed and power.

But are high-intensity runs actually messing with your hormones, or is the wellness side of the internet spreading misinformation? We’re here to separate fact from fiction.

Cortisol is a hormone made by your adrenal glands, which are located on top of your kidneys and are part of your body’s endocrine system.

“Cortisol helps regulate metabolism, blood pressure, and the immune response, and it makes energy available when the body is under stress—including during exercise,” says Dr. Aysegul Eren, M.D., endocrinologist and medical director of the Adrenal Program at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

This hormone rises when your body faces increased physical or metabolic demand, such as exercise, illness, fasting, low blood sugar, or psychological stress, Eren explains. During exercise, cortisol naturally spikes as a way to provide energy to your body so it can perform. Viewed through that lens, cortisol is an important part of your body’s response to exercise and your ability to complete workouts.

“Higher-intensity exercise reliably causes a temporary cortisol rise, generally related to exercise intensity,” Eren says. “This is normal physiology, not something harmful to prevent.”

How long cortisol remains elevated depends on the stressor, according to Dr. Feyza Erenler, M.D., an endocrinologist at Tufts Medical Center. It may be minutes to hours for a brief stimulus like exercise, she explains.

A 2021 meta-analysis of 10 studies on HIIT, published in the Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, found that cortisol increased immediately after exercise, often fell below baseline about two hours later, and returned to baseline within 24 hours.

“There’s no evidence that a specific number of HIIT sessions causes chronically high cortisol,” Eren says. “The more relevant concern is overtraining—chronic training without adequate recovery—which can lead to persistent underperformance. ‘Too much’ is individual, depending on training load, sleep, nutrition, recovery, and other stressors.”

In fact, research shows physical activity can actually lead to lower cortisol levels. A 2026 study in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that those who did 150 minutes of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise (50 to 85% of their max heart rate) every week for a year saw a reduction in long-term cortisol levels.

Symptoms frequently attributed to “high cortisol,” such as fatigue, poor sleep, anxiety, or difficulty losing weight, don’t indicate that a person has high cortisol, according to Erenler. “These symptoms are extremely common and nonspecific and can occur for many different reasons,” she says.

Signs of true high cortisol—not the brief, self-resolving spike during exercise—include bruising, muscle weakness (particularly in the upper legs), wide purple stretch marks, worsening high blood pressure or diabetes, and sometimes changes in fat distribution, according to Eren.

If you’re experiencing any of the above symptoms, Eren recommends discussing them with your healthcare provider rather than trying to diagnose yourself with high cortisol all on your own (or with the help of a chatbot). Chronic high cortisol levels that are undiagnosed can cause high blood pressure, diabetes, muscle and bone loss, higher infection risk, and cardiovascular complications.

But rest assured, cortisol disorders are rare. For instance, Cushing syndrome, a condition where you have too much cortisol in your blood for a long period of time, only affects 10 to 15 people per million each year, according to the Endocrine Society. Cushing syndrome is caused by a tumor on the pituitary gland at the base of your brain, not too much high-intensity exercise.

“During exercise, cortisol temporarily rises in response to the physiological stress and then decreases as the body recovers and the stressor resolves,” Erenler says. “In Cushing syndrome, cortisol exposure remains inappropriately elevated over time, and the normal regulatory mechanisms—including the normal circadian pattern and suppression of cortisol production—are disrupted.”

For most healthy people, there’s no need to try to suppress the normal cortisol response to exercise. Instead, the goal should be a sustainable training program that includes adequate recovery, sufficient sleep and nutrition, and variation in workout intensity.

“Don’t worry about the temporary rise in cortisol that occurs with exercise,” Eren says. “It’s a normal part of the body’s response to physical activity, not a sign that exercise is harming you.”

Erenler agrees and says the goal isn’t to eliminate cortisol—it’s to challenge your body appropriately and give it enough recovery to adapt to the stress you’re placing on it.

#8852. A 28-Year-Old Brooklyn Runner Died After Being Stabbed During an Evening Run. Police Are Still Searching for Her Attacker.

Katie Suarez’s death has left runners grieving and residents demanding better safety measures.

(Editor’s note: A 27-year-old man who worked for the city’s public school system was arrested and charged with the murder of Katie Suarez on Saturday, November 7, the New York Times reported.)

On Friday, October 30, Katie Suarez headed out at night along Brooklyn's Shore Parkway Greenway, a waterfront route she'd become quite familiar with from her regular runs around the neighborhood. The 28-year-old was stabbed in the neck that evening and died Monday, November 2, at NYU Langone Hospital-Brooklyn, her family confirmed.

The attack came just two days before the New York City Marathon, when the city was already buzzing with runners gearing up for Sunday's race. (Suarez was not registered for the event.) More than 60,000 people would be making their way through the five boroughs that weekend, but Suarez never got to finish her own run. Her death has since shaken the running community, particularly women who know all too well the safety concerns that can come with heading out alone.

Suarez usually met her parents after finishing up at the TD Bank near Caesar's Bay Shopping Center in Bath Beach where she worked, and joined them for the commute home. On the day of the attack, she switched into her running clothes and took off along the waterfront while her parents waited for her to return.

According to The New York Times, her father, Nery Suarez, called just before 8 p.m. to check on where she was. Katie told him she was only about half a mile away and would be back soon, but when more time passed without any sign of her, Nery and his wife, Yasira, became worried and went out looking for her.

Nery eventually found his daughter unconscious just off the running path near Bay 17th Street. She had suffered severe injuries to her neck and was rushed to the hospital, where she remained on life support until her death.

"I'm just left with this pain, and, oh my God, remembering my daughter as she was," Yasira told the New York Daily News on Tuesday. "She just wanted to run.”

As of November 6, police had not identified or arrested a suspect. NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny said Monday that investigators were still trying to determine what led to the attack, though they had no reason to believe Suarez was specifically targeted and "right now, it seems that it's random.”

Finding evidence has been especially difficult along the section of the greenway where Suarez was attacked, which is dark and has no reported surveillance cameras. Investigators have searched the surrounding area using everything possible, from drones to police dogs and scuba divers, while also hoping passing motorists might have recorded something useful.

"We are looking for Teslas, we're looking for Uber drivers," Kenny said, explaining that dashcam footage could help police determine whether the attacker crossed the Belt Parkway while escaping.

The lack of lighting has also brought up plenty of concerns from people in the neighborhood who regularly use the path. At a vigil held Wednesday night, neighbors gathered near the waterfront to remember Suarez and discuss what needs to change to make the area safer after dark.

"There's no lights anywhere. It's very dark. A lot of trees, can't see anything," resident Ann Florio-Lopez told ABC7 New York.

Another woman at the vigil said she'd already changed her routine because of the attack, telling the station she “stopped walking at night.”

Runners outside Brooklyn have been speaking up as well, especially with the attack happening so close to marathon weekend. Fast Women shared Suarez's story on Instagram, expressing disappointment that her death hadn't received more attention within the running community. The account also pointed to complaints from locals who had reportedly been asking for better lighting and security along the greenway for years.

For Suarez's younger brother, Christopher, running has taken on a new meaning. He told 1010 WINS that Katie was always looking out for him, often calling to check in whenever he wasn't home at his usual time.

Now Christopher wants to honor her by running “all the miles she wanted to run” and the races she’ll never get the chance to do.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

#8851. The Time of Day You Exercise Could Help Control Blood Sugar

Any physical activity is good for your metabolic health, but research says timing it right may have more benefits for your glucose levels.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Although blood sugar control is essential for those with diabetes, it’s also key for maintaining health overall. Research indicates that blood sugar levels can affect a range of physical functions, including hormone regulation, body composition, digestive processes, and even cognitive health.

That’s why keeping control of blood glucose levels is important, and one way to help might include doing moderate- to vigorous-intensity exercise in the evening, according to a study publish in Obesity.

Researchers looked at 186 men and women who were overweight or had obesity and were diagnosed with at least one metabolic impairment, such as high blood pressure or high cholesterol. Over a 14-day period, researchers tracked their physical activity and glucose levels, along with the time of day for exercise. Morning exercise was defined as before noon, with afternoon exercise between noon and 6:00 p.m, and evening exercise after that.

At the end of the two weeks, those who did more than 50 percent of their exercise in the evening had significantly lower glucose levels compared to those who were sedentary, and better glucose regulation than participants who mainly exercised in the mornings or afternoons.

The effects were especially notable for those who’d struggled with regulating their blood sugar before participating in the study, according to co-author Antonia Clavero Jimeno, Ph.D.(c), researcher in the department of physical education and sports at the University of Granada in Spain.

Although the study participants were specifically chosen based on metabolic factors and sedentary behavior, he told Bicycling that previous evidence has shown that the results might be the same for those without those factors, and who already exercise regularly.

“In fact, the impact of both physical activity volume and timing for glycemic control may be amplified in those with higher activity levels,” he said.

That’s backed up by previous research looking at active people who were assessed for blood sugar changes based on when they exercised. In that study, published in 2022, those who performed moderate-to-vigorous activity in the afternoon had 18 percent lower insulin resistance compared to morning exercisers, and the evening group fared even better, with a 25 percent reduction in insulin resistance.

One factor that was not explored in either study was the role of dietary changes, and this is an area that needs more research, said Clavero Jimeno. Determining whether a strategy like time-restricted eating—also called intermittent fasting—would be helpful or harmful to glucose regulation when paired with evening exercise is a next step, and is already being studied by Clavero Jimeno and his team. (Some research published this year suggests intermittent fasting may have promising effects on blood sugar regulation, at least in those with type 2 diabetes.)

“Dietary intake is, of course, recognized as crucial for glycemic control, and may influence the results overall,” Clavero Jimeno said. “But in the absence of that information, this current study does emphasize that if you want better control of your glucose levels, evening exercise, done at a higher intensity, may be beneficial.”

Here's the math that should stop you mid-scroll: a single night at a Category 4 Hyatt — think Hyatt Place in a major city or a solid Park Hyatt property in a secondary market — costs around $150–$250 in cash. Why rent-to-hotel is one of the most accessible travel rewards sweet spots

The core insight here has two parts, and understanding both will change how you think about every dollar of rent you pay going forward.

Part One: Bilt Is the Only Card That Earns Points on Rent With No Fee

Most landlords don't accept credit cards. Those that do typically charge a 2–3% processing fee, which instantly erases any rewards value. Bilt solved this by partnering directly with property management companies and creating a system where you pay rent via the Bilt app, and the payment processes as ACH (no fee to you or your landlord), while Bilt credits your account with points. You earn 1x point per dollar on rent, up to 100,000 points per year. On a $2,000/month rent payment, that's 24,000 Hyatt points annually from a bill you were paying anyway. Zero incremental spend. Zero fees.

The one rule to know: you must make at least 5 transactions on your Bilt card each statement period to earn points on rent. Five purchases — even five $1 transactions — unlocks the rent earnings. This is a simple, low-lift requirement.

Do: Watch for Hyatt's Points + Cash Awards

Hyatt offers a Points + Cash option at roughly half the standard award rate, combined with a cash co-pay. If your Hyatt balance is small, this lets you access properties without waiting to accumulate a full award.

This redemption was built for renters — specifically, renters who are already on the path to FI and feel the friction of paying rent every month with nothing to show for it. If you pay at least $1,000/month in rent, this sweet spot is generating meaningful Hyatt points from dollar one. At $2,000/month, you're accumulating 24,000 Hyatt points per year from rent alone — enough for two nights at a Category 5 property or a single aspirational night at a Park Hyatt.

Minimum to make it work: You need at least 5,000 Hyatt points for a Category 1 redemption — easily achievable after 5–6 months of rent payments on a $1,000/month lease. For aspirational Category 6–7 stays, you're targeting 25,000–30,000 points, which takes planning but is absolutely achievable.

This isn't the right fit if you own your home (no rent to earn on), if you're already deep into a competing hotel loyalty program, or if your primary travel goal is international business class flights — in that case, transferable airline currencies deserve more of your attention first. But for hotel stays, especially in the U.S., this is the single most frictionless on-ramp into the Hyatt ecosystem available anywhere.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness**, and that rating is accurate — but it helps to understand exactly *why* it's easy, so you don't accidentally make it harder than it needs to be. **What makes it easy:** - Earning is passive. Once your Bilt card is set up and rent is registered, points accrue automatically with no behavior change required (beyond five small monthly transactions). - The transfer is instant — no waiting, no uncertainty, no risk of availability disappearing while points are in transit. - Hyatt's award chart is fixed and transparent. You can see exactly what a property costs before you transfer a single point. - No fuel surcharges means no unpleasant surprises at checkout. **The one area that trips beginners up:** forgetting the five-transaction monthly minimum. This is the single most common Bilt mistake, and it's entirely preventable. Set up five small autopay charges on your Bilt card — a $5 streaming service, a recurring Amazon purchase, anything — and you'll never miss it. **Tip for the first redemption:** Start with a Category 3 or 4 Hyatt Place or Hyatt Regency for a domestic weekend trip. The points requirement is low (8,000–15,000 points), availability is widely open, and the booking process is identical to any other Hyatt stay. It's a low-stakes way to see the entire system work from earning to booking. If you can pay rent, own a smartphone, and make five purchases a month, you can execute this redemption. The ChooseFI community has embraced this one for good reason — it's genuinely the most accessible entry point into premium hotel travel rewards available today.

No. Bilt works with any landlord that accepts payment. If your building is not in the Bilt Alliance, Bilt processes the payment via ACH. The only difference is Alliance buildings may offer additional perks like bonus points or rent credits.

You will still pay your rent through Bilt, but you will earn zero points on that month's rent payment. The five-transaction requirement resets monthly. Set up autopay on small recurring charges to prevent this.

Yes. Bilt transfers to over a dozen airline and hotel partners including American Airlines, United, Air Canada Aeroplan, and IHG. However, Hyatt consistently delivers the highest cents-per-point value among hotel transfer partners.

Bilt caps rent earning at 100,000 points per month (equivalent to $100,000 in rent at 1x). For the vast majority of renters, this cap is irrelevant. There is no annual cap on total points earned.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Bilt-to-Hyatt pipeline is the most accessible travel rewards sweet spot available today. You are already paying rent. The Bilt card has no annual fee. Hyatt points deliver 2-8 cents in value. The transfer is instant. If you rent and you are not earning Hyatt points from that rent payment, you are leaving hundreds of dollars in annual hotel value on the table. Start with one Category 3-4 weekend stay to see it work, then scale up to aspirational properties as your balance grows.

#8849. The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”

The righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change. Often, the righting reflex is particularly strong in people who really, really care.

Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?

Motivational Interviewing describes how this (beautiful, well-intentioned) instinct to help can actually hinder a client’s progress.

That’s because when we swoop in to fix, correct, or steer, clients often do the exact opposite of what we’re hoping for: They dig in and get defensive.

Push someone the “right” way and, paradoxically, they’ll start advocating for the very habits they came to you to change. You end up being the one arguing for change—which leaves them to argue against it. Everyone walks away a little more frustrated, and the client feels more stuck than ever.

Instead, great, experienced coaches learn to get curious instead of corrective. (They might even encourage the client to explore not changing!)

That’s just one example of an upside-down skill that separates a good coach from a masterful one. But it’s certainly not the only example.

We asked some of Precision Nutrition’s most seasoned PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certified coaches a simple question:

What’s something you were sure about early in your career that you later had to unlearn?

Their (honest, and sometimes humbling) answers are below, plus the wiser way forward they adopted, and are now sharing with you.

Our first lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach Jeremy Fernandes, PN2-MHC.

With over 14 years of coaching experience, Coach Jeremy is known for his friendly, comfortable, “talk to me like I’m your buddy” coaching style. Which is ironic, because as you’ll see, he started off his career leaning heavily on a rigid structure that was actually pushing clients away.

At the beginning of my career, when I’d been a personal trainer for a year or two, I had a friend ask if I offered nutrition coaching. And my first move was: Here are all of the forms. And when I say “all of the forms,” I mean all of them—I probably sent this person 20 pages to fill out.

Three weeks later I had to hunt them down, and we ended up filling them out together—which took two and a half grueling hours.

If not for those forms, we could have started actually coaching, like, 20 days earlier.

Not long after, another friend showed up at my door with this white-hot intensity: “Tell me what to do, I’m ready,” they said. And I immediately dumped a metaphorical bucket of ice water on them with those darn forms. It was radio silence after that.

The problem was that I was operating like my sole job was to extract information from a person and then solve the mystery—as if I had some advanced pattern recognition about you that you didn’t have about yourself.

And unfortunately, I kept on that terrible path for a while.

What finally prompted a change was going through the Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

Going through that course, I saw there was a better framework—one that doesn’t rely on me robotically extracting information.

I learned to let the client take the lead, and then just listen and maybe ask a few good questions. And it works so much better—for everyone.

Now I work from the assumption that my client knows themselves better than anyone. One of my most valuable questions is simply:

“What have you tried before, what did you like about it, and what didn’t you like?”

When I let people take the floor, they nail the really big stuff more often than not—in a way my paperwork and my detective work never facilitated.

Honestly, the forms were me projecting professionalism, because back then I didn’t feel like a professional. My identity as a coach never felt natural until after L2. Now, just letting someone talk feels like coaching. We start with a connection, and then I just let them fill in the gaps.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN Director of Community Engagement and in-house coach Kate Solovieva, PN2-MHC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Kate is known for her honesty and incisiveness. She has a way of dropping realness on her clients that may first feel like a shock, but ultimately ends up getting her clients to the heart of the matter much faster. But one hard truth she had to face was her own.

You know the story: You reach the healthy weight, the habits lock in, and the weight just stays stable on its own. You hit “save” and move on with your happily ever after.

At least most of the time. It’s true, some goals really are like that. If you want to run a marathon, you can pick a race date, follow a training program, show up to the start line, run it—and then you never have to run again and you will still have achieved that goal. That’s a real destination; you cross the finish line once and check the goal off.

But weight loss, muscle gain, body recomposition, building a habit of movement or eating well—those aren’t like that. Especially when the goal means working against a chronic tendency, like a predisposition to high blood pressure, or to hating exercise, or to living in a larger body than you’d prefer.

Those goals come with a pretty good amount of ongoing and intentional maintenance—daily, weekly, monthly. There’s no save button.

This realization didn’t come from one single client or one moment for me. It came through a collection of observations, including observations of myself. But once I saw it, it changed how I coach.

I realized that if there’s no real finish line, then my job is to manufacture finish lines along the way. That way, my clients continually feel like they’re accomplishing something satisfying.

I take the big goal and break it into something specific and daily—and then I insert smaller outcome goals into the journey.

For instance, someone going from sedentary to wanting to lose 100 pounds is facing a huge goal, full of behaviors and identities they’ll have to grow into. So along the way, we might set a goal of running a single mile without stopping. Strictly speaking, that doesn’t have much to do with the bigger goal—but it also has everything to do with it. It’s checkable. Achievable. Ideally it’s also something they’re a little excited about: fun, interesting, maybe even a little scary, but still within reach.

Because here’s the thing: It’s very hard to motivate the human brain to work out three times a week for the rest of their life to “get healthier.” “Being healthy” isn’t tangible, it’s not immediate—you can’t feel that far-off outcome in your body.

But striving towards a fun, achievable goal in the next three to six months? That’s real. It also builds in structure, and provides those little spikes of motivation—the hit of dopamine you get from working hard at something and actually accomplishing it.

Health isn’t something we ever fully “accomplish” or check off. So we have to give ourselves these little concrete goals along the way that we can feel and see and be delighted by.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN content creator Azul Corajoria, CPT, PN2-MHC.

With over nine years of coaching experience, Coach Azul’s coaching fingerprint is empathetic, relatable, and endlessly encouraging.

While these traits always came naturally to her, for a long time, she thought she had to adopt an opposite style to help certain clients (and herself) to “get back in line” when habits didn’t go as planned.

Early in my coaching career, I thought that if someone wasn’t following through on what they said they would do, it’s because they needed more structure or just to get their “head in the game.”

I couldn’t understand why someone would invest in coaching and then not do the things we planned.

It was especially confusing because most of my clients had “discipline.” They were successful, responsible, hardworking people who showed up for their jobs, families, and everyone else in their lives.

Meanwhile, I was also “disciplined” in many areas of my life—yet I also struggled with eating well and exercising consistently.

At this time, I felt this lack of consistency was my fault, and went straight to being really angry at myself. I thought I was just missing the “perfect something” (the perfect workout, the perfect diet) to help me change, so I’d just move from thing to thing, but each one would bring fresh disappointment.

I was incredibly frustrated by this cycle, and my response was to get stricter and harsher with myself.

It’s hard to say when it all changed. It wasn’t an overnight epiphany; it was a culmination of years of getting curious, being open to different methods, like the Body Positivity Movement and Intuitive Eating. I dove into self-compassion and positive psychology research, and I went through the PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

I applied everything I learned, and I noticed that the more open and curious I was, the better my clients responded. Slowly, that turned into the realization that the more open and curious I was with myself, the better I would respond.

I stopped binge eating. I started enjoying exercise more. I took more career risks.

I learned that when we can respond to a setback with curiosity instead of punishment, we’re much more likely to stay engaged. When I allow myself to be disappointed by an action, take responsibility for it, and remain on my own side, I feel safer reflecting and taking risks. The more I do that, the more likely I am to achieve the things I want.

Sometimes the most helpful thing we can teach a client (and ourselves) is not how to push harder or “just be more disciplined.” It’s how to make a mistake, remain on our own side, and keep going.

Because self-compassion is not the opposite of accountability; it’s often what makes accountability possible. (I call it “compassionate accountability.”)

None of us will ever be the “perfect” coach, and we don’t have to be. The more human I’ve allowed myself to be, the better relationships I’ve had with my clients. My biggest goal as a coach is to create an environment my client feels safe to come back to with not only their wins, but their losses. The safer they feel being honest and open with me, the safer they’ll feel to try new things—and over time they’ll build the confidence to do it themselves.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Dom Matteo, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Dom stands out for his non-judgemental attitude and excellent listening skills. For Dom, these traits are relatively inherent, but they’ve also been carefully developed and honed, in part by letting go of what he calls the “coach’s ego”—the assumption that he already knew what a client’s success should look like, and that he was the one who got to keep score.

I took that stated goal at face value, and treated whatever number they gave me as the measuring stick, as the most important thing to work towards.

But then, I’d see a client struggling to do their actions even 50 percent of the time, and I’d think: ‘This person is never going to be happy, because this won’t get them to the goal weight they told me they wanted.’

Remember, I assumed the number was the real goal.

However, again and again, those same clients would turn out to be genuinely happy with their progress, not because they hit their exact goal, but because they felt so much better about themselves and their lives.

What I learned is that the stated outcome was almost never the true goal for many of them. When they said ‘lose 50 pounds,’ what they really meant was: I want to feel better. And being consistent even half the time, over a year, netted results they were thrilled with. Because they felt better. They felt different.

So the thing I had to let go of was my own scorecard. Who am I to tell a client that what they’re doing isn’t good enough, if they’re happy with how things are going?

My new definition of progress became less about approaching a specific final number and more about another question: “Am I a little better today than I was yesterday?”

These days, I spend time up front helping a client build what we call a “wellness vision.” We clarify their values, and what success actually looks and feels like to them.

Then, instead of assuming I know how to measure their progress, I’ll ask: “How will you know if this is helping? How do you want to measure success?”

The result is that even a client who’s fixated on the scale can see other signs of progress long before the scale actually changes. And often, those other signs are the things they really wanted to change in the first place.

It turns out the most useful thing I can provide isn’t a judgement about whether a client is succeeding. Instead, it’s to help them determine and notice their own success, by their own measures.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Jason Bonn, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 18 years of coaching experience, Coach Jason’s clients describe him as patient, observant, and deeply dedicated. He has a knack for spotting a client’s potential—though as you’ll read in this story, Coach Jason learned that getting too focused on a specific version of that potential sometimes kept him from seeing other ways his clients could grow and thrive.

For me, progress felt like a puzzle to solve: I’d play with adjustments to exercise volume or intensity, calorie or protein intake, eating more slowly, eating to 80 percent fullness, all the fundamental stuff.

But then, because of one client I still think about, I began to shift how I thought about “progress.”

He was in our PN coaching program. He lost 40 to 50 pounds in his first six months—which was great—but then everything stalled.

We tried adjustment after adjustment for the next two and a half years. We added more protein, more cardio, and worked through his particular peccadillo, eating corn chips at night. But none of it moved his numbers.

What got me was that he kept showing up anyway: three straight years, re-enrolling each time, even though the scale had plateaued.

That told me something was working for him—it just wasn’t something I recognized yet.

In his third year, we stopped looking only at the gym and his diet, and started looking at his whole life. He was a landscape painter, so we built his practices around that instead: make a sketch or work on a painting daily, anything that sparked some joy or interest. Within a couple of weeks, he was getting on his bike and riding out to further places for different scenery to paint.

In part because of this client, I’m now a lot more cognizant of coaching the whole person, and considering their Deep Health. Weight and performance numbers are just one piece of a much bigger picture that includes relationships, emotional wellbeing, and what someone finds meaningful.

I’ve also stopped zeroing in on “problem” behavior.

I try to understand a person’s life overall—not just the behavior I’ve been hired to help with—because there’s a connectedness to it all, and behavior tends to emerge within the context of someone’s life.

I’ve also stopped treating the coaching relationship as a means to an outcome and started treating it as the main thing—the sun that everything orbits, the glue that holds it all together.

That client kept coming back for three years because the relationship mattered to him. By the end, I’d stopped thinking I was failing him. The weight loss was such a small part of the success. The relationship was the bigger piece.

Coaching mastery isn’t about stockpiling more information. (Your clients can Google information or ask a chatbot, and so can you.)

It’s about developing the judgment to know when to use what you know, when to set it aside, and when the most helpful thing you can do is nothing at all, except be there.

But that kind of judgment is hard to build alone; it takes practice, expert feedback, and a few humbling moments with real clients—which is exactly what the PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certification is designed to offer.

With enough practice, self-awareness, and the right training, you can gain the wisdom and skill of the above coaches.

But the best coaches, it turns out, are defined less by what they know than by what they’ve been willing to unlearn.

Ready to move from competent to truly masterful—in 20 weeks?

#8846. The 9 Best Running Shoes for Runners With Flat Feet and Low Arches

No, you don’t need more arch support. But here’s what you do need.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 6, 2026: Our Best Overall, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25, is 19% off! Our team is currently testing the Adrenaline GTS 26, which is on sale now.

Shopping for running shoes can be especially frustrating if you have flat feet. There are conflicting opinions about what types of shoes best accommodate your foot shape. Some shoe brands add lots of arch support. Other experts say the opposite. What’s a flat-footed runner to do?

Despite the confusion, there are solutions out there, especially with flat feet being more common than you think. Finding shoes that work with your foot type, support good running form, and feel comfortable is paramount—and totally doable.

Not all flat feet are the same, which means there’s no universal solution that will work well for everyone. We’ll go over what it means to have flat feet and some of the potential issues the condition can present for runners. We’ve also highlighted shoe designs that might help alleviate any pain or discomfort you’re experiencing. Finally, we’ve picked the best running shoes for flat feet you can buy right now, including a wide range of options for walking, speedwork, trail running, and more.

Shopping for a daily trainer → Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 (Men’s/Women’s)On a budget → New Balance Ellipse (Men’s/Women’s)Searching for some stability → Hoka Arahi 9 (Men’s/Women’s)Adding speedwork to your training → Brooks Ghost Amp (Men’s/Women’s)In need of more cushioned support → Saucony Guide 19 (Men’s/Women’s)Curious about zero-drop → Altra Fwd Via 2 (Men’s/Women’s)Training to race → New Balance SuperComp Rebel (Men’s/Women’s)Racing a marathon → Hoka Rocket X 3 (unisex)Pavement-averse → Hoka Speedgoat 7 (Men’s/Women’s)

Runner’s World Running Reviews Editor Amanda Furrer—who has relatively low arches—researched shoe testing data from our team of approximately 300 wear-testers. Our program includes runners of various experience levels, paces, gaits, and, most important for this guide, arch types. They logged hundreds of miles in these shoes, evaluating comfort, fit, and ride.

Our contributors also gathered intel from industry experts. Caitlin Giddings consulted Kimberly Davis, DC, ART, who is CEO and founder of RunLab in Austin, Texas, and physical therapist Jay Dicharry, author of Anatomy for Runners. Both Davis and Dicharry have extensive experience assessing and treating runners of all experience levels, gait types, and footwear needs; they were able to provide significant insight on the topic. Michael Charboneau, former RW editor and freelance reviewer for InsideHook, Men’s Journal, and other publications, also offered his expertise in our Q&A section.

Shop the best flat-footed running shoe deals on Amazon

The Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is as much a runner-fave as its neutral counterpart, the Brooks Ghost 18. This updated version of the Adrenaline GTS features even more cushioning. Brooks heightened the forefoot 3 mm and the heel 1 mm, bringing the offset down from 12 mm to 10 mm. This means more of a balanced feel underfoot. The nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam provides a responsive, plush ride for everyday training and long runs.

Tester Peter Vuong, an overpronator with a flat arch, gave his seal of approval.

“This is a solid, all-around shoe with good flexibility, comfort, and a smooth ride,” he said. “I loved my runs in this shoe. It’s comfortable and laces up nice and snug. The fit is near-perfect. I tested it mostly on the road with a little trail. I would use this shoe for many occasions including a 5K race or nice Sunday 10-miler. It’s nice to have something for multiple uses like that.”

The shoe has the brand’s holistic stability guide rails system. Dense foam on the medial and lateral sides of the Adrenaline GTS act as “bumpers” to help align the knee and ankle when form gets erratic from overpronating. Testers said the fit and support were spot-on.

“I’ve run in just about every model of this shoe, many of them predating the guide rails system,” said tester Chris Garges. “This shoe provides the stability that I need as a heel-striking overpronator. I had no issues with the stability even later into a 14-mile training run. Some prior Adrenalines and the Glycerin GTS shoes seem to have a touch too much foot movement, particularly in warm, sweaty weather, which causes blisters or loss of toenails. I did not experience those issues with these shoes.”

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com

Think of the new Ellipse as your run club shoe; New Balance’s newest trainer is meant to make running easier with plenty of pop. The midsole is the brand’s Fresh Foam X, which ensures high energy return on your run as well as plenty of high-cushioned support that absorbs shock. It’s also a generous bed of plush for flat feet.

Testers praised the shoe’s cushioning, even though the ride for some felt slightly bulky. It’s not necessarily a speed shoe, but that didn’t stop some of our testers from going fast on that runner’s high. “It truly feels like I am at an advantage wearing these shoes,” said tester Laura Parks.

“The shoe is SO springy,” she continued. “The best word to describe the cushion is plush. I can feel my foot sinking into the cushion as it molds around me, while simultaneously still feeling the ground. The Ellipse has a cushy bounce sensation when I run in them that I haven’t quite felt before in other New Balance Fresh Foam models.”

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com

We loved the Arahi 8 so much we bestowed it Gear of the Year. The Arahi 9 preserved all we loved with a few key updates, making the shoe even better. The dual-density compression-molded EVA midsole is retooled so the ride is even softer and more supportive. Think of the new midsole as a plush bed of comfort for your flat feet.

Unchanged is the stability tech. The trainer formerly had the brand’s J-Frame, which was a dense piece of J-shaped foam that wrapped around the heel. The H-Frame, a dense H-shaped piece of foam used in Hoka’s beefier shoes, like the Gaviota, provides a more balanced ride without overcorrecting your gait.

The Arahi 9 kept the previous iteration’s streamlined design. The Hoka team tweaked the fit, making the upper provide more medial support. We like lacing up in this versatile trainer for everyday runs, fartlek workouts, and recovery days.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com

The Ghost Amp is a game changer for the Ghost franchise because you truly get the best of both worlds: the signature comfort Brooks is known for (and why we always recommend the Ghost to beginner runners) and propulsive PEBA foam to spice up your runs.

Unlike the Ghost 18, which has a narrower fit than previous iterations, the Ghost Amp has ample toe room in the toebox and an accommodating fit in the midfoot area.

We recommend the Ghost Amp for speedwork but our testers found the shoe works for all kinds of runs.

“I try to save these shoes for my speed days, but I can’t stop lacing them for other runs as well,” said editor and tester Monique LeBrun, who has flat feet. “When you’re a slower runner, like me, you don’t need a super fancy plated shoes to pick up the pace, lightweight well-cushioned shoes will do just fine. Also, the PEBA/EVA blend is soft and bouncy, and that helps me pick up the pace, but it also helps keep momentum on slower days or if I stop to walk.”

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com

Like many stability shoes these days, the Guide 19 provides support when you need it. The shoe has Saucony’s CenterPath technology, which uses higher sidewalls and a broader base to help stabilize erratic foot (and ankle and knee) movement. It also provides a locked-in, comfy fit that our testers favored for daily training and recovery runs.

The shoe has a slight rocker profile, which helps promote smooth heel-toe transitions on runs. Though the ride isn’t as responsive as other daily trainers (the Guide has Pwrrun foam, a proprietary EVA blend), it delivers a cushioned, yet supportive ride for collecting weekly mileage when you don’t feel like pushing the pace.

“Like its predecessor, this shoe made me feel good before even starting my runs,” said tester Dave Block. “I just love the comfort and feel! The shoe is very soft and slips on easily. I can’t think of any other shoe that feels this great, with the possible exception of the Adidas Pureboost, but that’s going back several years.”

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com

If you thought choosing to run in a low-drop shoe meant a non-supportive barefoot ride (not the ideal for runners with flat feet), then you’ve never run in the Altra Fwd Via 2. Formerly known for making exclusively zero-drop trainers, Altra has released low-drop shoes these past couple of years, welcoming the zero-drop curious into their fold.

Shoes like the Fwd Via 2 have a 4 mm offset, which is merely the height of two stacked nickels. This low heel-to-toe drop helps runners ease into running in this type of trainer without fully making the plunge to zero drop. The plush cushioning also helps with the low-drop transition. Your arches won’t feel sore due to lack of support thanks to the thick bed of Altra Ego P35 midsole foam, which reaches 37 mm in the heel.

Like all of Altra’s shoes, a wide toebox provides wiggle room. The shoe also has a slight rocker shape to promote propulsion.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

Think of the SuperComp Rebel as the successor to the SuperComp Elite v4, New Balance’s premium racing shoe beloved for its accessible features: a broader base, beefier cushioning for marathoners clocking over five hours, a rocker sole and carbon plate that’s propulsive but not too aggressive. The brand made the SuperComp Elite v6 snappier; it’s comparable to the Brooks Hyperion Elite 6. Though the SC Rebel is a “training companion” for longer efforts and carbon-plate conditioning, it’s also race day-worthy.

The midsole is the brand’s Infinion foam, which was featured in the max-cushioned 1080v15. The Infinion foam in the SC Rebel, however, is fine-tuned for springier, faster efforts.

“I enjoyed the energetic bounce I got running in these sneakers,” said tester Nina Rems. “My legs felt light and my feet felt quick. You definitely feel the difference running in sneakers with a carbon plate versus just foam soles. I was more responsive in these New Balance SuperComp Rebels than my regular trainers, New Balance 1080s.”

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com

The Rocket X 3 is Hoka-soft with all the super shoe features. The broader base makes this shoe’s fit and ride not as severe as competitors’. Our midfoot didn’t feel squeezed, our toes weren’t crowded, and corner turns didn’t cause our life to flash before our eyes. What you get running in the Rocket X 3 is a stable—but fast—racing experience.

The shoe has dual-density PEBA foam and a winged carbon-fiber plate. Even though its ride is not as aggressive as the brand’s other racing shoe, the Cielo X1 2.0, it still packs a bouncy punch for running half marathons and marathons, and offers plenty of cushioning so your body won’t take a beating hours on the road.

“I love the push-off,” said Erica Bobstein. “They are bouncy and springy and they allow you to propel yourself forward with less effort. They do not have the same speedroll effect as the Saucony Endorphin Pro, but rather have an explosive push-off that requires less energy.”

A combination of plush maximum cushioning and all the tech you need to stay upright on the trail is a winning recipe for flat-footed runners tired of staying on the roads. The Speedgoat gets a reworking with its seventh iteration, resulting in a more secure—albeit, snug for wide feet—fit, and midsole foam that provides comfort for ultra distances.

Toothy lugs provide grip and stability over mixed, technical terrain, while the Meta-Rocker geometry smooths out heel-to-toe transitions. The supercritical EVA foam is tweaked to add more pop on the trail.

Tester Diane Grim, who previously tested the Speedgoat 6, noticed a significant difference in the shoe’s bounce with the 7. She found the ride more forgiving, “which could be great for the long runs, less foot fatigue.”

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com

Some runners have anatomically flat feet, and other runners have what’s known as “collapsed arches,” which are flat because of a muscle weakness. Although the two types can look very similar, how you approach buying shoes for them varies widely, says Dr. Kimberly Davis of the RunLab, an Austin, Texas-based clinic that assesses running biomechanics and offers physical therapy and training.

Dr. Davis says that when it comes to shopping for a shoe for a flat-footed runner with collapsed arches due to muscle weakness, you can add arch support until the foot gets stronger and can support its own arch. But with an anatomically flat foot, arch support just sends stress up into the knee where it can lead to knee problems.

That’s why it’s important to know what type of flat foot you have before you settle on a shoe—and take into account not just your foot but your entire body, including knees, hips, and range of motion.

Added Arch Support Is Not Always the Answer

Runners with flat feet tend to overpronate, which is when the arches of the foot roll inward after landing. (This isn’t true across the board—there are plenty of flat-footed runners who are biomechanically sound and efficient, and don’t experience any overpronation.)

Up until recently, the running industry steered overpronators toward stability shoes to control this motion. Gradually, all that is starting to change with the realization that stability features don’t do much to correct the natural cycle of the foot, though some runners prefer having them.

Dr. Davis says people with flat feet often have really flexible feet that never get rigid for the push-off. “The footwear industry tries to solve that by putting an arch support in there to give them an arch or create suppination in the foot,” she says. “But that foot is structurally built that way, it’s not something you can solve with a shoe.”

Flat-Footed Runners Can Benefit From a Full-Contact Midsole

Jay Dicharry, author of Anatomy for Runners and director of the REP Lab in Bend, Oregon, agrees arch support can be detrimental because the arch is by nature dynamic, and having extra structure there can stop your foot from moving. Dicharry says flat-footed runners should put more focus on seeking out a shoe with a straight “last,” which is the mold that dictates the shape of the shoe. A straight-lasted shoe has a wider midfoot base and less of a cut-in, a profile that has fallen by the wayside in favor of hourglass-shaped shoes.

Most current shoes don’t provide much of a solid support surface for flat-footed runners, he says. “The problem is all these hourglass shoe shapes look nice on the wall, but when someone with a flat foot puts weight on one, part of their foot is bearing weight on the fabric upper,” he says. “The upper doesn’t work as a midsole for foot support. Feet do well when they’re on an even surface.”

The truth is most running shoes will work for most runners; however, if the shoes you’re using aren’t comfortable immediately or if you’re experiencing any pain while running, you should try a different pair. Get your movement pattern analyzed, whether at a clinic like the RunLab or even a running store that offers gait analysis.

Once you have more information about your feet and movement patterns, you can provide all that information to a running store to find the best shoe for you. Don’t be afraid to take a shoe out for a test run following assessment before purchasing anything.

Here’s a quick way to find out what kind of arches you have: Grab a piece of cardboard and head to the bathroom. Put the cardboard on the floor, wet the bottom of your feet with water in the bathtub or shower, then stand on the cardboard. If you see dry spaces where your arches are, you don’t have flat feet; if you see full footprints showing both soles, then your feet are flat.

As we noted in our explainer, there are multiple kinds of flat feet, and some feet are more flat than others. For a clear, detailed understanding of your foot shape and what kind of foot support you need, you should speak to a podiatrist or running expert.

How can I tell if I have naturally flat feet or collapsed arches?

People with naturally flat feet generally have the condition their entire lives. (Everyone is born with flat feet. Your arches develop in the first few years of life.) Collapsed arches are caused by muscle weakness or an injury. According to the Cleveland Clinic, the most common cause is “inflammation or a tear in the leg tendon (posterior tibial tendon) that supports the arch.”

Both naturally flat feet and collapsed arches can be painful, however, so if you’re experiencing discomfort, it’s best to consult with a doctor to determine which type you have.

My flat feet are causing pain and discomfort. What can I do to alleviate that?

Experts recommend stretching your Achilles, calves, and hamstrings. Stretching those tendons and muscles will help reduce strain on your feet. See our guides to strengthening and stretching the Achilles, calves, and hamstrings for specific exercises.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

Michael is a freelance writer with years of experience covering gear and the outdoors for Runner's World and other publications; when he's not writing, he's usually biking, hiking, and running in the mountains around Los Angeles, where he lives.

#8844. Unlock Your Full Potential by Fixing These Common Triathlon Body Imbalances

Triathletes can face muscle imbalances. These off-season exercises help build proper strength to prepare for next season. (Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete)

Triathlon training is all about repetition, with hours upon hours spent catching and pulling in the pool, turning the pedals on the bike, and turning the legs over on the run. With that repetition comes natural imbalance, with some muscle groups getting overworked while others get neglected (or even weaken with age).

Over time, these imbalances can impact performance directly or indirectly by contributing to injury development. That’s why taking time to identify and address these imbalances now will help keep you healthy in the long run.

By pinpointing areas of weakness or asymmetry early on, athletes can target the stabilizing muscles, improve biomechanical efficiency across all three disciplines, and significantly reduce the risk of overuse injuries that often arise from repetitive strain. Here’s how.

While swimming is generally thought of as the “safest” discipline in triathlon, issues can and do occur, often manifesting as “swimmer’s shoulder.” Swimmer’s shoulder is a bit of a catch-all term for pain in the front of the shoulder that encompasses several pathologies, including rotator cuff issues.

Typically, underlying laxity and instability exist. One factor that can contribute to shoulder problems is a strength imbalance between the shoulder internal and external rotators, with the internal rotators becoming disproportionately strong in comparison to the external rotators. This makes sense, as the shoulder internal rotators are active throughout the catch and pull, working to rotate the arm in and push against water.

But the external rotators still play an important role, as they help to stabilize the shoulder joint, keeping the ball of the joint centered in the socket to help prevent impingement and pain with overhead use and shoulder abnormalities. To decrease injury risk, external rotators should have about two-thirds of the strength of the internal rotators.

The most reliable, valid ways to check this involve specialized dynamometry equipment that measures force. But if you’re just looking to get a general idea, check how many reps of each of the below motions you can do until fatigue.

In this case, the test (lying prone, rotating the back of the arm up) can also be used as an effective strengthening exercise for external rotation. Start with higher reps, lower weights to learn the motion (3 sets of 10-12), then work up to higher weights, lower reps (4 sets of 6-8) to build more strength.

If this position causes pain or is too difficult at first, a side-lying shoulder external rotation is also a good option.

While the incidence of overuse injuries attributed to cycling is generally lower than those attributed to running, they can and do occur, most commonly impacting the knee and lower back. Although singling out contributing factors is difficult, the prolonged posture and muscle activations associated with cycling predispose athletes to overdeveloped quadriceps and an undeveloped posterior chain (glutes, hamstrings, back extensors) and lateral hip muscles.

Cyclists need strong quads – these are the predominant muscle used to power the pedal stroke. But the glutes and hamstrings do assist, so neglecting those leaves some power on the table. Plus, that injury-prone lower back needs adequate strength and endurance to withstand hours spent in a forward-flexed position.

Also, because muscle weakness and tightness often go hand-in-hand, related limitations in mobility throughout the posterior chain limit a cyclist’s ability to comfortably hold more aggressive aero positions. Those quads of steel will only help so much if you’re sitting up to ease back and glute discomfort by the end of a long ride!

The strength and endurance of the posterior chain (and also the lateral hip, which can play a role when it comes to knee pain on the bike) can be checked using a single-leg bridge hold.

The single-leg RDL is a good choice for eliciting both high force and stretch in the hamstrings and strengthening the gluteal muscles, back extensors, and lateral hips. Isolating each leg can also help with side-to-side imbalances.

When it comes to muscle strength and running, the glutes have been frequently implicated as the cause of (and solution to) many issues. But, while the glutes do play an important stability-related role in the run gait and deficits have been linked with injury, the true workhorse of the run gait – the calves – often gets overlooked and under-strengthened.

The soleus (one of the calf muscles) experiences forces of up to eight times body weight and produces up to 50% of forward propulsive power while running. Because the calves insert onto the heel via the Achilles tendon (which acts as a spring during running), the two are linked, with decreased calf strength seen in athletes with Achilles issues compared to healthy controls.

Strong calves can also help to protect against tibial bone stress injuries. Masters athletes lose calf strength (and Achilles tendon stiffness) disproportionately to other muscle groups with age, leading to both a reduction in propulsion and step length and an increased risk of lower leg soft tissue injuries such as strains and tendinopathies. So, when it comes to both performance and helping to guard against many common lower leg injuries, first check the powerhouse muscles below the knee!

Calf strength can be tested with a single-leg calf raise test.

The test here can again be used as the exercise – just load it up!

So, while the different disciplines and repeated motions of triathlon might lend athletes to certain imbalances, not all is lost! Triathletes can make themselves stronger, more resilient, and faster with some awareness and work – so don’t neglect those details.

#8843. The Best Cargo E-Bikes of 2026, Tested by Editors Who Used Them for Groceries, Kid Hauling, and Daily Commutes

From budget longtails to family-ready front-loaders, these picks can help replace car trips.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Each year, I ride many different bicycles. From high-performance road bikes to full suspension mountain bikes to basic hybrids, I’ve swung a leg over eight or ten styles of bicycles in the past six months. But switching to an electric cargo bike has made the biggest positive impact on my overall quality of life. Thanks to a cargo bike, I’ve been mostly car-free for the last several months.

Traditional bicycles are great for your daily commute, running errands, and cruising around. However, if you need to carry more than you can squeeze into a backpack or maybe some panniers, most commuter bikes or e-bikes aren’t up for the job. Common tasks like grocery shopping, carrying large items, or transporting children can be tough on even the best of them. That’s what makes cargo bikes great—they can carry everything (and more!) that you can imagine.

As their name suggests, cargo bikes are designed to carry heavy, large, or awkward loads. Their extra hauling capacity makes cargo bikes incredibly useful for families, commuters, and riders in cities, suburbs, and small towns across the country. Bicycle brands produce cargo bikes in several distinct layouts to meet the needs of riders seeking to carry or move more stuff by pedal power.

Almost any bicycle purpose-built to carry passengers or extra gear—such as packages, bags, or boxes—can be called a “cargo bike.” Cargo bikes typically feature reinforced frames, racks or mounting points, and come with higher payload capacities than traditional commuter, city, or townie bikes. Bike brands and third-party manufacturers also offer a wide array of accessories to outfit a cargo bike for your specific needs and use cases.

Bicycling’s editors are huge fans of cargo bikes, and we use them regularly for our daily commutes, running errands, dropping kids at school, and family rides. Like other bicycle types, cargo bikes come in all shapes and sizes—and there’s almost certainly one that’s perfect for you. Finally, while non-assisted cargo bikes are available, electric-assist cargo bikes are now far more common. So all of the models we test use electric motors.

Buying Tip: Consider where you will store your cargo bike. Their large size and extra weight can make cargo bikes difficult to store if you don’t have a garage or dedicated bike storage. If you need to park your cargo bike outside, get a heavy-duty bike lock and a bicycle cover to keep it safe.

Some cargo bikes are loaded with features but cost too much, while others are low-priced but don’t ride well. However, the Aventon Abound LR is the rare $2,000 electric cargo bike that doesn’t feel like a compromise—And that’s why it’s our Best Overall pick.

The Abound LR is built to handle daily life—daycare drop-offs and pickups, grocery runs, and commuting—without the premium price tag of its competitors. Plus, it rides with more polish than some bikes costing twice as much. This makes it a great option for families and utility‑minded riders. The LR can handle kids, panniers, and weekly shopping trips without stretching the budget. It’s ideal for those who value comfort and stability over top‑end speed.

If you’re comparing this Aventon to other electric cargo bikes, it feels more polished than budget longtails like the Lectric Xpedition 2.0 and Rad Power’s Rad Wagon 5. Yet, the Abound LR costs far less than premium mid‑drive cargo rigs from Tern, Cannondale, and Trek.

Many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Priced at $1,399 for the single-battery model, it’s one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes around. The dual-battery model ($1,799) boasts an incredible 120-mile range and a top speed of 28 mph. This makes the XPedition an option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike.

“The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, said Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers ($150) and the Essentials package ($120), I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”

However, concessions had to be made somewhere to reach this low price, and the result is a somewhat cheap feel. Most of the XPedition’s parts are bottom-tier—with the notable exception of the brakes. The pedal-assist motor is powerful off the line, but it is erratic at times. The XPedition is adequate if you live in a very flat area or don’t need to carry kids or an adult passenger. Despite these faults, if you’re on a budget and looking to ditch the car for errands and trips around town, the XPedition is the cheapest e-cargo bike we recommend.

Tern’s Quick Haul Long is enticing because it delivers the core functionality of the pricier GSD series at a lower price. While the Quick Haul Long’s frame isn’t as sleek as the GSD and lacks a suspension fork, the bike still has everything needed to be a true car replacement.

The Quick Haul features include hydraulic disc brakes, a robust double kickstand, a built-in frame lock, trailer attachment points, and an impressive maximum weight limit of 419 pounds. Tern also offers a wide range of accessories to customize the bike to your individual needs. Even when loaded with two kids and a trailer full of groceries, the Bosch Cargo Line motor handles the load with ease. However, don’t expect a speedy ride when fully laden. The bike can handle the load (and you’ll get where you want to go), but it won’t zip to its maximum pedal-assist speed of 20 mph when weighed down.

If you like the look, features, and price of Aventon’s Abound LR but want a smaller package, the SR is the bike for you. The SR has the same 440-pound carrying capacity and 60-mile range as its longtail sibling, but on a shorter wheelbase chassis. This makes it ideal for riders with space constraints (such as apartments and RVs) or anyone seeking a quick ride around town.

The Specialized Globe Haul ST packs 419 pounds of cargo capacity into a surprisingly compact frame. With powerful brakes, dialed geometry, and well-thought-out features, it’s ready for commuting, grocery getting, neighborhood errands, or getting a child to daycare. Without active suspension, the Haul relies on massive 3.5-inch tires for its ride comfort, which work well on all but the roughest roads.

My partner, Julia, purchased a Haul ST after reading the Bike of the Year review. She uses it for commuting in Boston and describes the Haul as zippy. She said, “The power levels are flexible, and I can easily adjust them to how I want to ride or tackle hills.” She also likes the cargo configurations for carrying groceries and running errands. Julia also likes the Haul’s geometry; “It’s nice to ride upright, and it gives me more visibility.”

The new third-generation HSD improves on its predecessor’s legacy. The HSD (short for “Haul Stuff Daily”) is a shrunken-down version of Tern’s GSD3 model released last year. The HSD3’s frame has a 419-pound carrying capacity (combined bike, rider, and cargo), added stiffness, and improved stability at speed compared to its predecessor. The P10e Sport configuration features the peppier Bosch Performance Line Sport motor and an electronic-shifting ten-speed TRP E.A.S.I. A10 drivetrain. The Sport motor’s 28mph assistance was a welcome upgrade for commuting and running errands alongside car traffic on local suburban streets. The 90 Nm of torque (15 Nm more than the standard Performance Line motor) also provides quicker acceleration from a dead stop and a little more oomph when loaded down with cargo or climbing hills.

While it’s the second-most affordable HSD3 model in Tern’s U.S. selection, the P10e Sport is certainly not a budget-priced e-bike. But for the extra cost over similar-sized cargo bikes, you get a proven and well-thought-out bicycle. The HSD’s features and design elements feel purposeful. A great example is the bike’s stowability: The HSD3 can be tilted and stored vertically, balanced on its rear rack. It also moves easily on its rear wheel when you need to park or store it. The handlebar and stem also fold down, making the HSD3 much easier to transport by car or SUV than almost any other e-bike.

The Fetch+ 4 is Trek’s take on the classic Dutch bakfiets. This bike is essentially the minivan of bikes—it carries up to four kids. It includes two child seats, but you can add accessories to improve your passengers’ comfort. These include a full cover for the basket to keep everyone out of the wind and rain. To power the Fetch, Trek uses Bosch’s BES3 system with a Bosch Cargo Drive motor. It delivers power via a Gates Carbon belt drive for virtually maintenance-free operation.

Most families know Radio Flyer for its iconic red wagons, tricycles, and ride-on toys, but did you know the company also made a range of electric bikes? I use “made” here because, unfortunately, Flyer is backing away from e-bikes to concentrate on its core business. However, if you buy this bike, you’ll still have after-purchase support and the brand will have spare parts available.

The Loop is a 20-inch-wheel mid-tail model equipped with a 750W hub motor (87Nm torque) and can carry up to two children as passengers. Like a good family bike, Flyer loads the Loop with safety features, including a fully enclosed rear wheel, long front fender, turn signals, and four-piston Magura hydraulic disc brakes. Flyer offers the Loop in one universal frame size (fitting riders 4’11” to 6’3”) and four color choices.

Health & Fitness Editor Monique LeBrun tested the Loop with her six-year-old daughter for several months. “I’ve never ridden an e-bike before, so I was a little skeptical about it, but I really enjoy riding the Radio Flyer,” she said. Lebrun notes that “the seat is very comfortable, and I love that it has a low frame so I can easily step on and off the bike.”

The Tern GSD redefines what a car-replacement bike can be. It’s easy to picture running errands on a cargo bike if you live in a city or a town with great cycling infrastructure. However, many people live in suburbs or other areas not exactly designed for bike commuting. The GSD’s Class 3 Bosch pedal-assist motor, massive cargo capacity, and solid battery range make long hauls realistic, even for riders who live miles from town.

Riders from 5 feet to 6’6” can share the same bike, thanks to quick-release adjustments on the seatpost and handlebar. The bar can even rotate forward for tall riders who want extra reach. The bike also features premium touches you won’t find on low-cost cargo bikes—like a suspension fork, Magura 4-piston hydraulic brakes, an integrated lock, and a suspension seatpost. Practical design details make storage and transport surprisingly manageable: the handlebar folds at the headset, the seat drops quickly, and the whole bike can be tipped upright to rest on its rear rack—perfect for tight garage corners. However, be aware that the GSD’s extra weight can make loading it into a vehicle a two-person task.

Do you need to carry absolutely everything and want to do it in style? If so, an Urban Arrow might be right for you.

This front-loader, basket-style cargo bike is designed for families and people carrying large items like multiple kids, large dogs (plural), a Costco run, or a couch—All things people can carry with an Urban Arrow. Thanks to its 75 Nm Bosch Cargo Line motor and 545Wh battery, it has the torque and range to carry you and your stuff up hills and to your destination without breaking a sweat.

Domestic and international cargo bike popularity has exploded in the past decade, says Xtracycles founder and longtail cargo bike pioneer Ross Evans. There are generally four main styles of cargo bikes: longtail, short-tail, front loader, and the bakfiet (a Dutch term that translates to ‘box bike’). You can also find trike varieties for riders needing to transport heavy loads or more than two children.

➡️ Longtail cargo bikes are the most agile and lightweight design. They transport cargo or passengers on an extended tail section behind the rider.

➡️ Short-tail cargo bikes are a variant of longtail bikes, but with a shorter rear extension that makes them more compact and better suited for those tight on space.

➡️ Front loader bikes place the payload in front of the rider, generally on a low-slung platform adaptable to suit many needs.

➡️ Bakfiet-style bikes feature a large basket (typically in front of the rider) for carrying cargo or transporting multiple passengers.

Moving hundreds of pounds on a bike without a motor is great...if you want to get a workout. But most riders and families don’t want that stress or extra work. That’s why we recommend electric motor-equipped cargo bikes. “Electricity and cargo bikes go together like PB&J,” Evans says. E-cargo bikes feature pedal-assist electric motors that can deliver more than 50 miles of range. This makes cargo bikes more accessible to riders who want car-like convenience in a bike-sized package.

However, the tech comes at a price: Electric cargo bikes are pricier than their non-electric counterparts. Unless you live somewhere completely flat, we think an e-cargo bike is the best choice. Electric motors vastly improve a cargo bike’s usability and can save you money in the long run by making it a more effective car substitute.

Once you’ve purchased a cargo bike, you’ll want the right accessories to maximize its utility. Start on the manufacturer’s website: Many brands sell panniers, racks, and child seats to match their cargo bikes. Alternatively, if your style is more “dump it and go,” bakfiets use a single spacious box—typically upfront—that’ll fit all your stuff (there are still seat belts for your kids). The best way to determine which style or bike you prefer is to take bikes for test rides.

Approach an e-cargo bike and accessory purchase the same way you would if buying a car. Try and test as many options as possible. Prioritize your most common cargo needs. While it can be fun to think in aspirational terms, a bike suited to your daily needs means you use it more often.

These bikes are thoroughly put through their paces by the Bicycling test team. We don’t only test them—we live with them. We haul groceries, drop kids off at school, and squeeze in as many rides as possible to see if these e-cargo bikes can truly replace our cars for daily life. Test Editor Dan Chabanov puts them through the ultimate car-replacement experiment on the streets of his hometown of Philadelphia, and Deputy Editor Tara Seplavy tests them on her daily commute to the office. A

t our Easton, Pennsylvania headquarters, the rest of the team gives these bikes a daily beating, using them to run errands around town (because let’s be honest—e-cargo bikes are just plain fun to ride). We also speak with the product managers behind the designs to understand their choices, and compare each model to its closest competitors to see how they stack up. Bottom line: we test these bikes like we’d use them in real life—because we actually did.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.
