#8793. The Benefits of Biking for Seniors, Including the Mental and Physical Payoffs

You might find a few surprising advantages of cycling on this list.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

We know you think we’re going to tell you all the ways cycling improves your heart health and muscle strength—and it does, but guess what? According to a 2023 scoping review in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living, studies show that when older adults cycle regularly, their happiness improves and they are better able to maintain their quality of life.

In fact, even though many people associate aging with physical and mental declines, regular exercise—like a daily bike ride—can help slow or even reverse some of these effects.

“Regular physical activity helps seniors maintain good health, improve their quality of life, and increase their overall well-being,” Mary Sabat, MS, RDN, a personal trainer and dietitian in Georgia tells Bicycling. “It can enhance physical strength, flexibility, and endurance, making it easier to perform daily activities and maintain independence.”

Those are just few reasons why biking for seniors is so great—but here are all the advantages you gain when you start pedaling regularly.

While almost forms of physical activity improve physical and mental health, cycling is particularly well-suited for those in their golden years due to its accessibility. After all, cycling is easy on the joints, even for those with joint pain or injuries. “It can be tailored to individual fitness levels and adjusted to accommodate different abilities and physical limitations, too,” says Sabat. “Recumbent bikes, trikes, or electric-assist bicycles can be used to make cycling more accessible for those with mobility challenges or balance issues.”

Robert Patterson, a cyclist and lawyer, has been cycling for more than 40 years. He points out all the obvious aerobic and strength-building gains he’s enjoyed over the years, but also the psychological benefits. “Cycling also benefits my mental health. My attitude and overall focus are always improved by being on the bike,” he says.

Here are nine reasons, according to the experts, for you to saddle up and hit the road (or the gym) for a ride.

Aerobic exercise is the key to managing heart health. Because the heart is a muscle, it needs to be exercised on a regular basis to maintain its strength and optimal function. And because the heart and lungs work together with the venous system to deliver oxygenated blood to your muscles, any exercise that increases your heart rate and breath rate for an extended period of time will help improve your heart health and overall cardiovascular function.

Plus, as anyone who has ever pushed the pedals and pumped through a 20- or 30-minute bike ride knows, cycling will definitely get your heart rate up. The repetitive cycling motion qualifies as a moderate to intense form of aerobic exercise that you can easily adapt to your personal fitness level. This means that even if you haven’t exercised in years, by starting at a lower intensity and making adjustments to your workouts based on your heart rate, you can safely and effectively add cycling to your weekly routine.

“As individuals age, the risk of heart disease increases,” says Sabat. “Cycling is a low-impact aerobic exercise that helps improve cardiovascular fitness, strengthens the heart muscle, and enhances blood circulation. It can lower the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and high blood pressure, thereby promoting a healthy heart.”

In fact, a series of two 2019 review studies (part 1 and part 2) published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found that all forms of cycling reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and also reduced the risk factor profile for poor heart health—meaning that cyclists had better body composition stats, blood lipid profiles, cardiorespiratory fitness levels, and more time spent exercising. All of these together help mitigate the risk for developing heart disease.

You can combat practically any chronic condition, including heart disease, along with type 2 diabetes, arthritis, and cancer with a regular ride. Exercise helps keep the blood flowing, systems moving, and cells turning over in a way that promotes overall health. For instance, high-intensity exercise (and high-intensity cycling, specifically) helps improve blood glucose response, according to research, which may reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Even in the case of cancer, participating in a regular cycling routine has been shown to reduce the risk. For example, May 2020 study published in The Lancet found an association between participating in a daily bike commute and a 16 percent decrease in cancer mortality and an 11 percent decrease in cancer incidence.

“By incorporating a ride here and there into their routine, seniors can reduce the risk of chronic conditions. These conditions can be debilitating, but with regular exercise, seniors can take proactive steps toward prevention and management,” Josh Weight, a certified sports physiotherapist and the director of Gravity Physio in Australia tells Bicycling.

It’s not unusual for seniors to experience regular joint pain associated with arthritis or previous injuries. In fact, according to the National Poll on Healthy Aging, about 70 percent of older adults report current joint pain. This can be exacerbated by extended periods spent sitting, or simply not moving around much, as sedentary behavior is directly associated with increased incidences of knee and other joint pain.

While on the surface this may not seem like a big deal, it can lead to a cascading series of events where joint pain or arthritis contributes to a reduced range of motion. This reduced range of motion can influence balance, coordination, and even the ability to perform everyday tasks. These issues can also contribute to a reduced quality of life and even an increased risk of falls. As such, any activity that can be done without contributing to joint pain while protecting and strengthening the structures that help stabilize the joints (muscles, tendons, and ligaments) is an important undertaking for older adults’ overall health and well-being.

“Cycling is a low-impact activity that puts minimal stress on the joints, making it an excellent option for individuals with joint-related issues. It provides a cardiovascular workout without placing excessive strain on the knees, hips, or ankles,” Sabat says.

Whether done on an indoor bike or a more traditional road or mountain bike, one thing’s for sure: Cycling works the legs. It takes muscular strength, power, and endurance to keep the pedals moving, especially when climbing a hill or ramping up the resistance. But it’s not just the legs and glutes that benefit—cycling can help build strength in the shoulders, upper back, and core, as well.

Of course, you may not be looking to build massive quads as one of your long-term fitness goals, but developing muscular strength isn’t just about looking strong—it’s about maintaining your quality of life.

Research estimates muscle mass begins to decline by 3 to 8 percent every decade following your 30th birthday, with those rates increasing further once you hit 60. This age-related muscular decline over time makes it more challenging to continue doing everyday activities like climbing stairs or carrying groceries. It’s important to participate in exercises, like cycling, that will help maintain or build muscle mass over time to safeguard your ability to perform these daily activities.

In fact, according to a 2015 review study published in the European Review of Aging and Physical Activity, adults over 70 years of age experienced increased muscular strength and power when participating in a cycling exercise program at least three times a week for 12 to 16 weeks. This data flies in the face of anyone who believes they can’t develop muscle or strength as they age—it’s not only possible, it’s critical to overall health and functional ability.

One area in which cycling can be particularly beneficial is balance and coordination. This has ties to muscular strength, as strong, trained muscles tend to perform and react more quickly to stimuli than those that aren’t worked regularly. However, it also has to do with the unique requirements of cycling itself.

“Cycling requires balance and coordination to stay upright and navigate,” says Andrew White, a personal trainer and owner of Garage Gym Pro. “This can be especially beneficial for seniors as these abilities tend to decline with age, increasing the risk of falls and injuries.”

This isn’t just conjecture—a 2018 prospective study published in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity found that older adults (between the ages of 65 and 85) who cycled daily had better balance, a faster pace while walking, and better self-reported lower-extremity function compared to those who didn’t bike regularly. Based on this study, it appears that cycling helps preserve balance and coordination which contributes to lower-body function that can help prevent falls.

Just as muscle mass tends to decline with age, an associated change in body composition takes place, which often leads to increased weight gain. And as weight creeps up, so do the risks for heart disease and chronic illness, particularly in populations considered obese.

Cycling and other forms of exercise can help keep weight and other disease risk factors in check. This is partly due to the muscle-protective benefits exercise offers, but also due to the increased calorie burn that occurs during moderate- to high-intensity exercise like cycling.

“Cycling can help seniors maintain a healthy body weight, reduce excess body fat, and prevent obesity-related health issues,” Sabat emphasizes.

It’s not unusual for seniors to experience social isolation that can contribute to physical and mental health decline. Changes in health, mobility, or driving status can keep seniors alone at home. This is unfortunate because strong social connections are positively associated with longevity.

Cycling can provide seniors with an accessible way to get out and about, and to also engage with other people of all ages. “Cycling can be an enjoyable and social activity for seniors. Exploring outdoor trails, participating in group rides, or engaging in community cycling events can foster a sense of camaraderie and connection with others,” says Weight.

And for seniors who want to start cycling, but don’t know how, community cycling clubs offer a great way to learn and connect at the same time.

In addition to the benefits of social interaction, cycling can boost mental health in a number of ways, especially if you’re riding your bike outside. “Cycling outdoors provides an opportunity to connect with nature, which can be therapeutic and stress-relieving,” says White.

In fact, according to a 2022 study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, individuals who participated in outdoor cycling (or other outdoor activities like walking, jogging, or team sports), were less likely to experience depression than those who were inactive. Likewise, there’s evidence that even a single outdoor exercise session (like cycling) can impact mood, more than indoor exercise equivalents.

Even in the absence of an outdoor setting, physical activity as a whole is good for mental health. “Regular exercise releases endorphins which can elevate mood and reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression,” Sabat explains.

One final benefit of cycling for seniors: It can support cognitive function. “Studies have shown that physical activity can have positive effects on cognition and may help reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older adults. Exercise promotes better blood flow to the brain, stimulates the release of hormones that support brain health, and improves memory and attention,” Sabat shares.

Laura Williams, M.S., ACSM EP-C holds a master's degree in exercise and sport science and is a certified exercise physiologist through the American College of Sports Medicine. She also holds sports nutritionist, youth fitness, sports conditioning, and behavioral change specialist certifications through the American Council on Exercise. She has been writing on health, fitness, and wellness for 12 years, with bylines appearing online and in print for Men's Health, Healthline, Verywell Fit, The Healthy, Giddy, Thrillist, Men's Journal, Reader's Digest, and Runner's World. After losing her first husband to cancer in 2018, she moved to Costa Rica to use surfing, beach running, and horseback riding as part of her healing process. There, she met her current husband, had her son, and now splits time between Texas and Costa Rica.

#8792. Our 30 Unwritten Rules of Triathlon

Tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know. (Photo: Challenge Family)

Like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules. For example, you’re not allowed to cut the course, have a motor on your bike, curse at officials, punch a rival, or, most craven of all, have fewer than three safety pins on your race number in France.

However, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of. Some of them, we’ve helpfully outlined below:

1. Procrastination is Expensive — Swear you’ll sign up at the early bird rate, procrastinate, and then find out your chosen Ironman sold out within 24 hours anyway.

2. Forever Alone — The training paradox. The more you do triathlons, the more all your friends are triathletes, and the more you will train alone.

3. You Are Not Kristian — The Norwegian Method is to train more hours in a day than you do not train. For more training methods, see YouTube.

4. The Devil’s in the Details — Dedicate 20 hours a week to training for three months in the lead up to your A race. Spend zero minutes working on transition.

5. Shelve Twitter Hate — Write a mantra on your water bottle and start an Instagram account for reels, stories, and collabs. Don’t be an angry person on Twitter. That’s not cool.

6. Match at All Costs — Never sacrifice style for performance. Color-coded kit and equipment are essential, unless you’re going for garish retro, which is an acceptable look for 2026 only.

7. Weather or Not? — Check the weather forecast and water temperature before checking the weather forecast and water temperature, and then solicit opinions on what the weather and water temperature are likely to be on race day.

8. Wetsuit Your Worries Away — Convince yourself you can’t swim without a wetsuit/won’t be able to get your wetsuit off if it’s a wetsuit swim.

9. Experience Equals Complacency — The athlete guide must be studied with a focus that inversely correlates to how many races the athlete has done.

10. Selfie First, Reality Later — Take a selfie with the giant M-Dot “Ironman Is In Town” sign. Post this to social media as soon as you land, feigning a smile because although you’ve arrived, your bike hasn’t yet followed.

11. Hell’s Bells — Set three alarms minimum and then wonder why the first of them is going off as you force-feed yourself rice because you couldn’t sleep anyway.

12. Nothing Matters as Much as Everything — Take time to stare at your race tattoo, realize the transfer has only half stuck, and have a mild panic by convincing yourself you’ll be disqualified before the start.

13. Apply Liberally — Use sunscreen, making sure you miss a key patch of skin. It will show more of your suffering.

14. Pay it Forward — In the name of karma, offer to: a) Zip up someone’s wetsuit; b) Lend them a bike pump (even if it’s not yours); c) Thank everyone you see profusely and wish them all a great day.

15. Ride the Intake Earthquake — Increase your volume of carbohydrates per hour exponentially with the same dedication you had when you raced 15 years ago and were insistent on using only your 5% body fat as a fuel source.

16. Be a Bathroom Banterer — Talk with bravado about your trained ability to both pee in the swim and on the bike while you stand for an hour in a revolving porta potty line.

17. What’s Good for the Goose is Good for the Gander — Oops! You punched someone in the eye in the swim completely by accident. Also, the breaststroker you got stuck behind at the first buoy deliberately kicked you in the face.

18. Meditate on Aquatic Paradoxes — During the swim, reflect on: a) Whoever learned to swim as a kid is basically a cheater. Or b) “Why do triathletes swim so freaking slowly?”

19. Style Reigns — Replace existing drink bottles on the bike with those from the on-course sponsor. Call bottles bidons if you’ve ever watched a clip of the Tour de France.

20. The Refs Need You (Really) — Become militant about drafting and shout obscenities at a pack who: a). Aren’t in the race anyway; b) Are out for a gentle social weekend ride; c) Are still moving faster than you.

21. Ride the Highs and Lows — When you are riding downhill, you think you will win. When you are riding uphill, you think you will come last.

22. Roll the Dice — Breathe a sigh of relief when you complete the bike leg without puncturing because you haven’t practiced changing tires for five years.

23. Don’t be Patronizing Pat — If you pass someone on the run, resist the urge to tap them encouragingly on the back. One athlete’s chirpy come-on is another athlete’s patronizing pat. And if you must do it, always avoid the backside.

24. Leave Self-Awareness Back at the Hotel — Do something in the finish chute that in any other walk of life you would find cringey. This includes sweaty mess marriage proposals to a long-suffering partner who has a cooked neck from staring at a race tracker for the past 14 hours.

25. Be Congratulating Carl — Always congratulate the first person you see at the finish. However hollow-eyed your expression or soiled your tri suit. It’s your duty to have that mutual moment with a complete stranger.

26. The Rules of Race Photography are Unbending — Acknowledge that official race photographs only ever capture: 1. Grotesque faces. 2: When you “briefly” sat up out of aero. 3. Ugly heel strikes

27. You’re the Best — Use multiple filters of the race results, including but not limited to age-groups, disciplines (including transitions), and nationalities to claim a top-10 position at some aspect of your race. If you rode a road bike, you can also disqualify everyone who rode a TT/tri bike.

28. Brutality Reigns — Include the word “brutal” at least three times during any social media race report.

29. There Are Steps — Once you have finished your first sprint triathlon, take the following actions (in order): a) Sign up for an Ironman, b) Sign up for a Hyrox, c) Advertise your coaching services.

30. Triathlon = Procrastination (Always) — Finally, swear you’ll sign up at the early bird rate, procrastinate, and then find out your chosen Ironman sold out within 24 hours anyway.

Picture this: you're settling into a fully flat bed on an Iberia Airbus A350-900, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Spanish wine in hand, Madrid a few hours away. The cabin is quiet, the seat is wide, and you're sleeping your way to Europe in genuine business class comfort. The person next to you in economy paid $900 for their ticket. You paid $900 in cash too — except your $900 covered taxes, fees, and a couple of nice dinners in Madrid. The flights themselves cost you 34,000 Iberia Avios. That's the magic of this redemption, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community light up: a round-trip business class ticket from JFK to Madrid on Iberia regularly retails for **$2,500 to $5,000** in cash. At the off-peak Avios rate of **34,000 points one-way**, you're extracting **7.4 to 14.7 cents per point** — a figure that puts this redemption in a completely different category from most loyalty redemptions, where 1–2 cents per point is considered standard. To put that in human terms: if you transferred 34,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Iberia Plus and used them for this booking, you'd be getting a value equivalent to someone handing you a $2,500–$5,000 check in exchange for points that cost you roughly $340–$510 in credit card spend to earn (at a 1% earn baseline). That's not a deal. That's a pricing inefficiency, and it's one that's been hiding in plain sight for travelers who only know British Airways Avios and never discovered Iberia's **separate, more generous award chart**. The FI mindset is about finding asymmetries — places where the value you receive is wildly disproportionate to what you give up. This is one of the cleanest examples in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. You're not gaming anything. You're simply using Iberia's published off-peak pricing to access a premium cabin product that most people assume is out of reach. Your future self, lying flat at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, will be glad you learned this system.

Europe in a lie-flat seat for fewer points than most domestic first class awards

Here's the insight that separates travelers who occasionally use points from those who systematically fly business class to Europe for nearly free: Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency, but they operate on completely different award charts.

Most people who've been in the travel rewards world for a while know about British Airways Avios. They know that BA prices awards by distance, and they know that BA is notorious for hefty fuel surcharges that can turn a "free" business class flight into a $700+ fees bill. So they write off transatlantic Avios redemptions as not worth it.

That's the mistake. Iberia — a fellow Oneworld carrier and Avios partner — publishes its own off-peak award chart for flights operated on Iberia metal (Iberia aircraft, Iberia flight numbers). Flights from the US to Madrid, when booked through Iberia Plus (not British Airways Executive Club), price out at 34,000 Avios one-way in business class during off-peak periods. That's the same Avios currency, same points you can transfer from Chase, but priced under Iberia's more favorable structure.

The fuel surcharge situation is also materially better on Iberia-operated flights booked through Iberia Plus than BA-operated flights booked through BA. Taxes and fees are generally moderate — you're looking at a few hundred dollars in fees rather than the $600–$700+ that sometimes plagues British Airways award bookings.

Off-peak windows are specific. Iberia defines off-peak as January through March and October through November. Mark those months. Outside of those windows, pricing steps up, and the sweet spot math starts to erode.

The transfer path is straightforward. Iberia Plus is a 1:1 transfer partner with Chase Ultimate Rewards, and transfers are instant — a critical advantage when you're chasing limited award availability. You search, you find the seat, you transfer, you book. No waiting 3–5 days for points to land and watching the seat disappear.

Marriott Bonvoy is also a transfer partner (3:1 ratio, 1–5 days), but the math there is less favorable and the speed is slower. Chase Ultimate Rewards is your primary earning vehicle for this redemption.

One important structural note: Avios are shareable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts — meaning if you've been accumulating BA Avios, you can move them to an Iberia Plus account to access Iberia's off-peak pricing. This opens the door even if you've been building your Avios balance through the British Airways credit card or BA partners. The accounts need to be linked through the Avios household account feature, but it's a powerful tool that many travelers overlook.

Finally, keep the expiry rule in mind: Iberia Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A single small transaction — even buying a few Avios — resets the clock. Don't let your points die quietly in an unused account.

If you don't already have one, go to iberia.com and sign up for a free Iberia Plus account. This takes about five minutes. Write down your membership number — you'll need it for the transfer step. Make sure your name matches your passport exactly to avoid issues at check-in.

Go to iberia.com and select "Book with Avios" in the award booking section. Enter your route (e.g., JFK to MAD) and select your travel dates. Critically, target off-peak months: January through March, and October through November. These are the windows where the 34,000 Avios one-way business class pricing applies.

Search one-way first. Iberia's search tool will show you available Avios seats color-coded by price — you're looking for the off-peak pricing tier. If you see 34,000 Avios for business class, that's your seat. Note the specific flight number and date before doing anything with your points.

Before transferring a single point, click through the booking to see the full taxes and fees. Iberia charges moderate fees on transatlantic awards — generally more reasonable than British Airways — but you want to know the number. Confirm you're comfortable with the cash portion before proceeding.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal at ultimaterewards.com. Navigate to "Transfer to Travel Partners" and select Iberia Plus. Transfer exactly 34,000 points (or the amount required for your specific itinerary). Transfers from Chase to Iberia Plus are 1:1 and instant — your Avios will appear in your Iberia Plus account within minutes.

Go back to iberia.com with your Iberia Plus account logged in. Confirm the award seat is still showing (it should be — you moved fast). Complete the booking using your Avios balance. Pay the taxes and fees with a card that earns well on travel or general spend.

Award space on popular routes can be tight. Here's how to improve your odds:

Most airline programs charge the same award price year-round or use dynamic pricing that moves with demand. Iberia is unusual because it publishes an explicit off-peak calendar with fixed lower pricing during specific date ranges. Off-peak pricing applies to the flight date, not the booking date, so you can book an off-peak flight months in advance and lock in the lower rate. The off-peak discount is roughly 50% compared to peak pricing on the same route. This creates a planning advantage for flexible travelers who can target specific travel windows. Combined with the fact that Avios transfer from five major credit card programs, it is one of the most accessible premium redemptions in the loyalty landscape.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers are concrete.

It's mid-October — peak fall travel season for most Europeans, but squarely within Iberia's off-peak award window (October through November). You've found award space on IB6251, JFK to MAD, departing John F. Kennedy at 10:30 PM and arriving at Madrid Barajas the following afternoon. The aircraft is an Airbus A350-900 — one of the best long-haul platforms in the sky.

The cash price for this flight in business class: $3,200 one-way, as priced on iberia.com for that week. Round trip in business runs approximately $4,800–$6,000 depending on timing.

The Avios price: 34,000 Iberia Avios plus approximately $250–$350 in taxes and fees.

Your CPP on this redemption: With a retail value of $3,200 and a cost of 34,000 points, you're extracting 9.4 cents per point — comfortably in the 7.4–14.7 cent range that defines this sweet spot as exceptional.

Now let's talk about what you're actually getting for those points. Iberia Business on the A350-900 features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration — meaning every passenger has direct aisle access. No climbing over a seatmate at 2 AM. The seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 73 inches. You'll have a personal entertainment screen, noise-canceling headphones, and amenity kit.

Before you board, you have access to Iberia's business class lounge at MAD (on the return) and partner lounges at JFK — typically the Iberia-operated space or a Oneworld partner lounge. The meal service on this transatlantic route reflects Spanish hospitality: proper courses, wine service, and a breakfast before landing.

For a couple traveling together, this redemption costs 68,000 Avios plus fees — a round figure that's very achievable through the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus alone. You land in Madrid rested, having slept in a flat bed over the Atlantic, having spent a fraction of what cash passengers paid. That's the FI travel rewards system working exactly as it should.

Do this: Book as close to 355 days out as possible for off-peak dates. Iberia releases award space up to 355 days in advance. The most reliable business class availability appears right when that window opens. If your target is January or February travel, set a calendar reminder for April or May of the prior year and search on Day 355. The seats won't last.

Do this: Transfer Avios from a BA account if you've been building there. If you've been earning BA Avios through the British Airways credit card or BA shopping portal, you don't need to start over. Avios are transferable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts via the household account feature. Link the accounts, move the Avios to your Iberia Plus account, and access the off-peak pricing. This is an underused feature.

Do this: Earn points primarily through Chase Ultimate Rewards. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, and Ink Business Preferred all feed into the same Chase UR pool with a 1:1 instant transfer to Iberia Plus. For this redemption specifically, Chase is your most efficient earning engine. Use the welcome bonus from one of these cards as your foundation — a 60,000–100,000 point bonus gets you most of the way to two one-way business class seats.

Avoid this: Transferring points before confirming award space. Avios are transferred into Iberia Plus and can't be easily moved back or transferred to another program without complexity. Always confirm the exact flight, date, and availability BEFORE you initiate a transfer from Chase. The instant transfer speed from Chase means you can lock in availability quickly — but only once you've verified the seat exists.

Avoid this: Booking during peak periods expecting off-peak pricing. December, July, and August are not off-peak. The 34,000 Avios rate is specifically tied to Iberia's off-peak calendar (January–March and October–November). Outside those windows, pricing increases significantly and the CPP math deteriorates. Don't assume off-peak pricing applies year-round.

Do this: Keep your Iberia Plus account active. Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you're holding points for a future redemption, keep the account alive with a small transaction — even earning a few Avios through a partner purchase resets the clock for another 36 months.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want to experience genuine transatlantic business class — flat beds, real meal service, lounge access — without the $3,000–$5,000 cash outlay that normally makes that choice feel irresponsible on a FI journey.

You're a great fit for this redemption if:

This is also an excellent gateway redemption for families with older children who understand that off-peak travel timing is part of the strategy — though booking four or more business class seats requires significant Avios accumulation and tighter award availability.

For the FI community member who's disciplined about earning and has a Chase UR foundation, this is one of the cleanest business class sweet spots available anywhere in the transatlantic market.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty** — not because anything about it is technically complex, but because it requires you to navigate a few specific steps that most people haven't done before. **The main challenges are:** 1. **Awareness of the separate Iberia award chart.** Most travelers default to British Airways Avios and never discover that Iberia prices its own flights differently. Once you know this, it's not a challenge — it's an advantage. 2. **Award availability.** Iberia business class award seats on JFK–MAD are genuinely limited, especially as you get closer to the off-peak windows. You're competing with other knowledgeable award travelers. Availability is rated a 3 out of 5 for a reason — the seats are there, but you have to work for them. 3. **Account setup.** You need an Iberia Plus account separate from any BA account, and you need to navigate iberia.com's award search interface, which is functional but not as polished as some other programs. **Three tips to overcome these challenges:** - Search award space **355 days in advance** for maximum selection - Use **iberia.com directly** to search — it shows Iberia-operated availability most accurately - Keep the **Chase UR instant transfer** in your back pocket so you can act the moment you find space If you've ever transferred points to an airline and booked an award flight before, this will feel familiar. If this is your first time, expect to spend an evening learning the process — but the payoff is a flat-bed seat over the Atlantic for a fraction of its cash price. That's worth an evening.

Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency and can be transferred between accounts for free. However, Iberia's award chart prices flights on Iberia metal differently than British Airways does. For flights to Madrid on Iberia-operated routes, booking through Iberia Plus is typically cheaper than through BA Executive Club.

No. Iberia's off-peak pricing applies only to Iberia-operated flights. British Airways has its own separate pricing structure through BA Executive Club. For flights to London, you would need to use BA Avios and their own award chart, which does not offer the same off-peak discount.

Yes. Iberia updates its off-peak calendar periodically, and the specific date ranges can shift by a few weeks. Always check the current published calendar before planning your trip. The general pattern of January-March and October-November as off-peak has been consistent, but exact boundaries vary.

Iberia long-haul business class features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration with direct aisle access on their A350 and A330 aircraft. The seats convert to a flat bed for sleeping. The food and wine service reflects Spanish culinary traditions, including Iberian ham and regional wines. It is a solid European business class product, comparable to Air France or Lufthansa.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Iberia Avios off-peak business class to Madrid is the most efficient way to fly business class to Europe on points. At 34,000 Avios one-way, it costs less than many domestic first class awards. The off-peak calendar rewards flexible travelers with a 50% discount, and the breadth of transfer partners means almost anyone with transferable points can access this redemption. If you can align your European travel with the off-peak windows, this sweet spot delivers exceptional value with minimal complexity.

#8788. Warrior 2 Teaches You to Balance Effort and Surrender

(Photo: Andrew Clark; Design in Canva by Laura Harold)

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about how to do Warrior 2 Pose first appeared in the May-June 2000 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Over two millennia ago, one of the most essential teachings of yoga was given on a battlefield, of all places. As recounted in the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna, the consummate warrior, becomes paralyzed with doubt and fear just as he is about to be called to action. Luckily for him, his chariot driver happens to be none other than the god Krishna, who proceeds to reveal to Arjuna the teachings of yoga to liberate him from his confusion.

In my favorite translation of the Gita, by the late scholar/teacher Eknath Easwaran (Nilgiri Press, 1985), Krishna defines yoga as “wisdom in action”—yogah karmasu kausalam (II.50). He guides Arjuna to reflect upon the source of his actions and find his internal center, where he is free from the fluctuations of the mind.

Many centuries later Mahatma Gandhi would take these teachings of the Gita as guiding principles for his life.

Gandhi saw the battlefield as a metaphor for our internal conflicts and Arjuna as the archetypal warrior within—one who sees through illusions to the truth and is able to act with courage and unwavering focus. Perhaps as a beginning yoga student, you have already encountered a glimpse of this warrior spirit in the standing pose Virabhadrasana II (or Vira II for short). In the deep lunge and open arms of this Warrior Pose variation, there is a challenging intensity—a marked contrast to the images of yoga as a passive practice intended for relaxation.

You may ask, “Why is there a Warrior Pose, when yoga is a practice of nonviolence?”

As a strong pose, Virabhadrasana II can teach modern yogis a lot about the dynamics of bringing wisdom into the actions of our everyday lives. It is a powerful pose, no doubt, but as you explore the pose’s alignment and inner attitude, the heart of the peaceful warrior begins to reveal itself.

As we go about our daily lives, we often speak of feeling “off-centered” or of needing to “get centered.” Being “centered” is a feeling of being balanced and at ease on all levels—physically, emotionally, mentally, spiritually.

It is the clear space of awareness from which the wise action within any moment can be found.

To find your center in Virabhadrasana II—the place where your energy is distributed evenly, without bias—start by grounding yourself within Tadasana (Mountain Pose). The training of a spiritual warrior begins here as you let go of any external distractions and bring your awareness to your core.

When you feel your mind settle within the relaxed steadiness of Tadasana, then prepare to begin Virabhadrasana II. Consciously step your feet apart in a wide stance (4 to 5 feet), with your heels aligned parallel to one another. Pivot your left foot out to a 90-degree angle and pivot your right foot in to a 45-degree angle. Plant your feet like roots, connecting through all of the corners of your feet while lifting through the arches.

To focus on the leg work of Virabhadrasana II first, keep your arms relaxed at your sides. Slowly bend your left knee until it comes directly over your ankle. Now explore the feeling of your weight. Is all of your weight in your front leg? Lunge deeper into your left leg and then shift your weight into your back leg to feel the extremes, and then try to find the balance point.

Let your left hip sink to draw you deeper into the lunge, but keep your right leg firm, inner thigh lifting, and outer edge of your right foot reaching into the ground. As your legs develop stamina and your hips open, you can begin to explore coming into a right angle with your front leg as if you are balancing something on your thigh.

Once you find the place where your weight is evenly distributed through your legs and hips, bring your awareness to your torso. Are you collapsing into your lower back? Find your vertical center by turning your tailbone toward the earth. Without tension, lift your lower belly, the seat of your power, towards the spine. This action will awaken your center, so you can begin to extend out of your lower back and spread your chest open. Now balance your rib cage directly over your pelvis. Is your torso turning towards the left leg? Draw your right side and the top of your right thigh back to feel yourself opening out from the center.

Keep scanning your body to feel where you are losing awareness and balance. Change sides and explore Virabhadrasana II to find that even flow of energy—north, south, east, and west—throughout the pose.

As a metaphor for living, yoga can help us see how unnecessary tension within our actions shifts us off-center. To maintain Warrior Pose, we often harden our eyes, hold our breath, or shrug our shoulders. Try Virabhadrasana II again on the left side, setting up your foundation from your center. Slowly raise your arms up to shoulder height, keeping your shoulder blades pressing into and down your back. Now, turn your gaze (drishti) to the middle finger of your left hand.

Like a Zen archer spotting a bull’s-eye, who practices just holding a bow for two years before ever releasing an arrow, find balance within your focus by becoming inwardly detached.

Let the backs of your eyes look inside while you stay totally present. Feel the power of your energy radiating freely from your center. Find the balance between working to your full potential and completely relaxing, mirroring the effortless stillness of an eagle hovering over a current of wind.

As you explore this dance between being active and receptive, you can contemplate Krishna’s paradoxical teaching, “One who can see action within inaction and inaction within action is the wisest among all beings.”

As you look out from this still point and open your inner ears, you may hear your internal warrior teacher giving you insights to bring you into balance not only in this moment, but in your life as a whole. Like Arjuna as Krishna whispered over his shoulder, you may be given confidence to face your fears, courage to move forward, compassion to embrace another, and wisdom to surrender to the one who holds the reins.

#8787. The 8 Best Altra Running Shoes for Runners Who Hate Cramped Toes and Want to Try Zero-Drop

Altra is known for its women-specific fit, wide toebox, and zero-drop cushioning. We recommend the best Altra shoes—including those with a 4mm offset—out now.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 10, 2026: Need some support trying low drop? The Altra Experience Form is now 24% off—but inventory is low, so stock up now!

Altra holds a special place in my heart because one of the first shoes I reviewed after I was hired at Runner’s World was the brand’s now-discontinued Instinct/Intuition 4.5. Altra was founded in 2009 by high school running buddies Golden Harper and Brian Beckstead. Turns out the Instinct/Intuition was pivotal to Altra establishing itself in the running industry. It was the first model Altra launched in 2011.

Since my introduction to Altra, I’ve witnessed its evolution; the brand formerly known for strictly selling zero-drop shoes (when forefoot and heel cushioning are equal) has added models with a 4mm drop. This move has drawn the zero-drop-curious to the Altra way.

Looking for a zero-drop daily trainer → Altra Torin 9 (Men’s/Women’s)

In need of stability → Altra Experience Form (Men’s/Women’s)

Curious to try low-drop → Altra Experience Flow 3 (Men’s/Women’s)

Shopping for a low-drop trail shoe → Altra Experience Wild 3 (Men’s/Women’s)

Racing a marathon → Altra Vanish Carbon 3 (Men’s/Women’s)

Logging long runs → Altra Fwd Via 2 (Men’s/Women’s)

Wanting a true racing flat → Altra Escalante 5 (Men’s/Women’s)

A lover of gnarly trails → Altra Lone Peak 9+ (Men’s/Women’s)

Balanced Cushioning, which refers to the shoe’s heel-to-toe drop, or lack thereof. Altra designs most of its shoes with no drop, meaning your foot sits flat rather than sloping downward from heel to toe. According to Altra, this can help promote your natural stride and encourage a lower-impact landing—because the heel isn’t as beefed up, you’re less likely to land on it.

Altra also introduced its 4mm line of shoes so runners can ease into zero-drop with an offset that’s approximately two stacked nickels.

The first time I ran in Altras, I couldn’t help feeling like I was wearing clown shoes. Unbox a pair of Altras and you’ll see that the forefoot is much wider than on other shoes; the enlarged, anatomical toe box allows the foot to expand and gives the toes room to splay. Altra now has three different foot shapes: original (the widest), standard, and slim (the narrowest).

Wide-foot runners and runners with bunions appreciate the roominess in the toe area. But all runners can benefit from wearing Altra’s foot-shaped trainers. A narrow toebox that cramps your toes can negatively affect your performance (and set you up for injuries).

The company uses three main cushioning materials in its shoes: Ego, Ego Max, and Ego Pro.

Ego: Compared to traditional EVA, this foam provides a springier feel and more durability.

Ego Max: A foam made of compression-molded EVA and tuned for a softer feel than Ego, but it isn’t as responsive.

Ego Pro: Altra’s top-shelf foam made of thermoplastic elastomers (TPE) formed in a supercritical fluid process. It’s the brand’s lightest and most responsive cushioning material.

P35X: Altra’s new and improved version of Ego foam that’s lighter and more efficient.

Altra’s stability tech is its guide rail, which is a layer of dense midsole foam that is raised on the medial side. The guide rail serves as a “bumper” that helps counter overpronation during your stride.

Altra’s women’s shoes are built on a women’s-specific last to match the biomechanics of female feet. These shoes are narrower through the heel and midfoot and better accommodate women’s generally longer arches.

Since my introduction to Altra as a new hire at Runner’s World in 2018, I have tested several models by the brand, appreciating the shoes’ generous toe room on my wide feet. I have tested all of the shoes in this buying guide and delved into the feedback of our 350-plus shoe testers. These local runners present an inclusive testing pool, ranging in gait patterns, arch heights, and experience levels.

*All weights are for men’s 10 and women’s 8.

The Torin has undergone a revamp with its ninth iteration—but rest assured, all these changes are welcomed upgrades.

The shoe has a new Vibram outsole, which inspired our testers to take the shoe off the road and onto the trail. “I felt that the shoe performed best on a packed dirt/trail surface where it felt like it had a great traction and springy push off. Those trail runs were at a 7:00 to 7:30 pace,” said tester Steven Blasi.

On the road and off, the Torin 9 is bouncier and softer too. Altra’s P35X midsole makes for a more cushioned ride without silencing ground feel. The support makes the shoe a great entry into zero-drop for newbies.

Lastly, the fit is more accommodating. The non-gusseted tongue provides a roomier fit for those with high insteps.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

The Experience Form provides stability when you need it with Altra’s guide rail. Acting as a “bumper” on the medial side, the feature lends support to overpronators and neutral runners, alike.

“I liked the overall stability and comfort of the shoe,” said Anthony Dentino, a heel-striker who runs with a neutral gait. “The shoe was firm but provided excellent cushioning throughout, especially in the heel. Because of its weight, this is not a shoe that I would suggest for speedwork or racing but it is an excellent training shoe.”

Another favorite feature was the shoe’s hardiness and trustworthiness in inclement weather.

“I wore them multiple times in the rain and on some snowy surfaces, but felt like they provided good traction every time,” said overpronator Alyssa Dever. “Not only that, they did not soak through easily in the rain, and kept my feet warm in cold temperatures (some sub-20-degree runs).”

Shop Men’s at rei.com Shop Women’s at rei.com

If switching to zero-drop still sounds like taking a major leap, you can opt for running in the Experience Flow 3 before you go for a spin in the Torin 8. The Experience Flow has a 4mm offset, which is approximately the same depth of two nickels stacked on top of each other. The heel lift is subtle, allowing you to ease into running in a low-drop shoe.

Testers loved the versatility of the shoe, appreciating its supportive Altra Ego midsole. For some, it hit that Goldilocks sweet spot of feeling not too firm, nor too soft.

“I loved that it was a not a minimalist shoe, but wasn’t the huge cloud cushion kind either,” said tester Chris Greg. “It was a happy medium between the two where I felt connected to the ground but was offered plenty of support to make my 5-mile runs smooth.”

Others described the cushioning as having just the right amount of “squishiness.”

“I really loved how much cushioning these shoes had,” said tester Mary Hartnett. “It made my runs feel so much easier and ‘squishier’ compared to other shoes I’ve used. This extra softness was a huge help during my training because I actually felt excited to put them on every morning, and my feet didn’t feel as tired afterward.”

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

We’ve loved the Experience Wild since its first iteration. The shoe is outfitted for technical trails, offering protection with a toe sweep, gaiter attachment points, and a grippy MaxTrac outsole that can handle loose, uneven terrain. It’s also a great option for those who run on bridle paths and groomed rail trails. The Experience Wild 3 is flexible, has an accommodating wide fit in the midfoot and toe area, and a padded tongue that makes the fit snug and enclosed, so pebbles and sand can be kept out.

The biggest update to the Experience Wild 3 is the mesh upper, which provides a more secure fit and more breathability.

“V3 takes the shoe to the next level with a redesigned upper that fits more generously but doesn’t make you feel like you are swimming around, a more plush cushioning that absorbs firmer ground yet remaining stable, and a lug pattern on the MaxTrac outsole that I felt was superior to each of the previous models in terms of grip,” said tester John Mikovits.

The Experience Wild 3+ ($165) is also available and has a Vibram Megagrip outsole.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

The Vanish Carbon 3 feels like a true super while preserving Altra’s fit and feel. The racing shoe is the first in its line with a 4mm offset; the Altra shoe team realized their super shoe needed a drop so they wouldn’t be outmatched by competitors. Altra’s running economy tests showed the Vanish Carbon 3 had 2.6 percent better running economy compared to the Vanish Carbon 2.

A carbon plate is sandwiched between FastRce, which is pure PEBA. The plate has a split big toe to allow for engagement and power. All this is housed in an upper with Altra’s signature roomy toebox that provides generous wiggle room for your toes to splay.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

As of updating this buying guide, I only just laced up in the Fwd Via 2 after meeting with Altra at the Runner’s World Shoe Summit before the NYC Marathon. The original Fwd Via was an instant favorite from first run. The shoe has a rocker profile and high cushioning, making the low heel-to-toe drop easier to get used to if you’re a zero-drop virgin. It’s great for long runs and recovery runs, and has a generous bed of foam for run/walkers.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

It’s been two and a half years since the release of the Escalante 4—but the Escalante 5 makes that length of time worth the wait.

Nothing has dramatically changed with the Escalante 5: same roomy toebox, same breathable knit upper, same Ego midsole, and same 24 mm stack height. Instead of fully revamping the shoe, the Altra team refined it with a few tweaks.

The strobel and sockliner are made of TPEE for even more comfort. In this way, you still get plenty of ground feel in this minimalistic, lightweight trainer, but with added comfort and support. The outsole also has more rubber to enhance traction and durability.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

The Lone Peak 9+ is the first iteration of the shoe with a Vibram Megagrip outsole. This makes the shoe have outstanding traction on wet or dry surfaces. RW Tester feedback confirms Vibram Megagrip’s traction on uneven, slippery terrain.

Said tester Shelby Brett, “I greatly appreciate that the lugs on the shoe are significant and that they go in multiple directions, again adding to my confidence underfoot.”

The shoe has a durable ripstop upper and an extra eyelet for a more locked-in fit. Testers loved the ground feel of the Lone Peak 9+, saying the shoe had the perfect balance of cushioning and protection. Another highlight was that spacious toebox.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

We recommend starting slow and short if it’s your first time running in zero-drop shoes. Shoes with a drop have more cushioning in the heel. If you’re a heel-striker, you may need to run in a zero-drop shoe with a higher stack height to provide more support under the heel area. Try Altra’s 4mm shoes first to become accustomed to a lower-drop shoe.

What is the difference between Altra’s guide rail and Brooks’s guide rails?

Altra’s guide rail runs along the medial side of the shoe, acting as a bumper and preventing your foot from collapsing during sharp turns or if your feet roll inward during your gait cycle (overpronation).

Brooks’s guide rails are on the medial and lateral sides of the shoe. Like Altra’s guide rail, the guide rails also provide stability when you need it, making the shoes supportive for overpronators and neutral runners. The guide rails act as bumpers, helping align the knee and ankle.

#8786. Our Editors Ride-Tested Virginia Tech’s Top-Rated Road and Gravel Helmets—Including a $60 Pick That Punches Way Above Its Price

Lab safety scores matter, but so do fit, ventilation, and price. Here’s how the top lids compare.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times. Unfortunately, I’ve also had a few concussions. Because of this, safety is important to me when I choose a new helmet. Over the last few seasons, I’ve tested dozens of great helmets, from budget picks under $50 to go-fast aero lids and lightweight models for over $500. Plus, I also test trail helmets, commuter lids, and everything in between.

When shopping for new road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort. Depending on our riding goals and budget, we also balance weight, aerodynamics, and style. We want safety features, but many riders assume most helmets do a decent job of protecting our noggin—they’re all certified, right?

Helmet safety isn’t as straightforward as it may seem. Current Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standards—as well as more rigorous, voluntary requirements, such as those from ASTM—account for straight-line impacts and G-forces from a collision. These standards don’t address the rotational forces from a crash that contribute significantly to concussions and traumatic brain injuries. Plus, the CPSC’s standards took effect on March 10, 1999—advancements in technology, design, materials, and manufacturing over the last 27 years have changed bike helmets.

So, what standards and certifications cover rotational forces? Currently, none. To better protect against rotational forces and reduce concussions, many brands incorporate Mips liners (and similar anti-rotational designs) into their helmets. Brands also test their helmets internally to their own, generally unpublished, criteria. The Virginia Tech helmet lab’s STAR score provides the best independent testing and ranking for helmets across most cycling disciplines.

Virginia Tech tests helmets for safety; it doesn’t evaluate fit, comfort, weight, price, or overall practicality. Bicycling’s test team collectively rides tens of thousands of miles each year on tarmac, gravel roads, singletrack, and commuting. That means we have a lot of time to ride-test lids—including more than half of Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR-rated road helmets.

For 15 years, Virginia Tech has tested helmets through a battery of 24 impact tests that analyse safety performance and assign an overall STAR (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk) score.

“The overall score estimates the number of concussions the average person would see if they experienced identical impacts at rates matching their weightings while cycling,” says Virginia Tech’s lab. The lower the STAR score, the better a helmet performed in testing.

Then, to each helmet it tests, Virginia Tech awards an overall STAR rating (one through five); helmets with four- and five-STARs are “recommended.” The lab does not recommend helmets scoring three STARs or fewer.

Virginia Tech has tested and published results on more than 300 bicycle helmets. To date, the lab has awarded 56 helmets its coveted 5-STAR rating, and another 104 received 4 STARs. To make researching and choosing a new helmet easier, it also sorts the helmets it tests into mountain, road, urban, multi-sport, full-face, and E-bike categories. Of the 5-STAR helmets, 21 of them are road lids.

Editor’s Note: These helmets are the top 5-rated road bike helmets in Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet rankings as of November 9, 2026. The Virginia Tech helmet lab regularly tests helmets and updates the overall rankings; the top 5 can change at any time. Please consult Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet ranking list for up-to-date rankings.

“Who is Pikio?” and “What is a Si Oblik?” Those were the questions our editors all asked when we saw this helmet rocket to the top of Virginia Tech’s STAR ratings. The Pikio isn’t only the top-rated road helmet; it’s also Virginia Tech’s best-performing helmet, period. It beats the others by a considerable margin, logging an unbelievably low 4.61 STAR score. For context, the difference between the Pikio and the second-place overall Canyon Deflectr RLS mountain bike helmet is 2.21 points; that’s the same gap between the 2nd and 28th positions in current rankings.

All of that safety comes at a relatively steep $379 cost. While the Si Oblik’s price aligns with other range-topping helmets from Giro, POC, Specialized, and MET, Pikio’s looks and finish feel comparable to mid-tier models from more well-known brands. For example, Pikio’s color options are somewhat conservative choices, and the rear strap anchor point is through-shell.

The Si Oblik fits well and has a broad range of adjustment for my medium-sized head. The rear adjusts up and down (to account for head shape and hairstyles) and features a dial to microadjust fit. The straps, however, are not as cleanly executed as expected for the price, especially compared to POC or Specialized, and I found them slightly tedious to adjust. On road and gravel rides, the Si Oblik’s airflow doesn’t feel bad, but I didn’t test this lid in peak summer heat. And while the Pikio weighs about the same as Giro and MET helmets in this test, it feels physically bigger, though not as mushroomy as the POC Cytal.

For a new brand, Pikio Labs made a solid first effort. Unlike its competitors, Pikio doesn’t have decades of trial and error or a flashy WorldTour team. Hopefully, as the company grows, it can dial in details, sharpen pricing, and spice up the aesthetic, because the Si Oblik already sets a very high bar for safety.

The POC Cytal’s unique shape and bold look make it easy to spot in a peloton. Another reason the Cytal stands out is due to its overall size—it’s a physically big lid. But despite its dimensions and slightly heavy weight, it doesn’t feel that large on your head while riding and ventilates surprisingly well.

The Cytal’s great ventilation comes from its massive vents and internal air channels that funnel air directly over your forehead while riding. I found out how well it vents while riding over the summer in France during “la canicule” (the heatwave). I could still feel the Cytal pushing air in 100-degree temps, even if it was roasting hot.

In our recent review of P2R’s $100 aero-helmet, ride tester Tom Messina said it “has no business being this good.” And with its lower price and STAR score, we say the same thing about P2R’s $60 A20 Mips. With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price.

P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road.

The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it on said it was a little snug near their temples.

Given the Trenta 3K Carbon’s pedigree, it’s hard not to name it “Best for Racing.” UAE Team Emirates’ official sponsor is MET, and the Trenta is one of the helmets it supplies to the squad—including Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they sometimes pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. At over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit.

Ranked 14th overall and 5th in road helmets, Giro’s Aries Spherical stands out in our testing for its overall comfort, adjustability, low weight, and great looks. While its STAR score is much higher than the first-place Pikio, the Aries is a very safe helmet and received Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR rating. Having crashed on the road while wearing an Aries Spherical, I also know this helmet works.

Of the approximately one dozen road and gravel helmets in my rotation at any given time, I reach for the Aries Spherical most often. The Aries fits my head perfectly, and the Roc Loc dial system offers plenty of adjustability for hair length or if I’m wearing a cap underneath in rain or cold weather. Giro makes the Aries in a wide range of colors and graphics to fit almost any rider’s personality or fashion.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8785. Turn Your Pool Workout Into Playtime With These Game-Inspired Exercises

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Turn your swim workouts into games with these fun ideas for making the pool more enjoyable. (Photo: Challenge Family)

We know all the excuses to skip a swim because we’ve used many of them ourselves. Either it’s too cold outside or it’s too beautiful a day to pass up a bike ride. Or perhaps there’s a storm 100 miles away that might suddenly decide to blow right over the aquatics center. But the truth is, if your workout is interesting enough, you’ll have all the excuses you need to get yourself into the pool, not out of it.

And we’re not just talking about adding in a random drill here and there. Gamifying your swim workout, whether through solo exercises or team activities, helps make a workout enticing enough that you’ll want to do it over and over again. Adding an element of play to your swim can make it more challenging, productive, and fun all at once.

Before we get into a handful of our favorite games and drills, we asked Sage Hopkins, head coach of Women’s Swimming & Diving at San José State University, for his tips on how to make swimming more enjoyable. With these tools in your arsenal, you might not skip your pool workouts anymore, but actually look forward to them instead.

First, Hopkins stresses how crucial it is to hear laughter echoing across the pool deck. This might not be possible if you’re training alone, but if you have a training buddy who always keeps you smiling, make it a priority to meet with them more regularly. Hopkins also encourages using music to establish an upbeat atmosphere; that might look like playing a pump-up song on your way to the pool, or investing in a pair of swimming headphones to keep the tunes going lap after lap.

Once you know your purpose, Hopkins says, it’s easier to figure out what kinds of activities will make swimming more meaningful and enjoyable. Those who enjoy the camaraderie aspect of swimming and triathlon will enjoy team games like sharks and minnows.

Even simple details like naming a set, Hopkins says, can add a thrill to swimming. If there’s a test set you’re always dreading, give it a quirky or amusing name to make it seem less intimidating. You could use the most challenging triathlon you’ve ever lined up for as inspiration (The Wales One Hundreds, for instance, or the Norseman No Breathers).

Now, without further ado, let the games begin!

You don’t need any fancy clubs to play a round of swim golf — just enough glycogen in your head to add numbers. Hopkins suggests this drill for data-driven triathletes because it’s easy to keep track of your progression over time. Essentially, you add the number of strokes with the number of seconds that it takes you to complete a certain distance (such as 50 yards) to get a “score.” You’ll then repeat that distance several times within a single set, trying to keep your score as low as possible. This game helps improve your distance per stroke and ultimately conserve energy.

Healthy suspense invites bursts of dopamine and curiosity into your workout, and it also means that there’s no one to blame but fate for back-to-back sprint sets. Make sure to write the following rules down on a whiteboard or protected piece of paper to reduce confusion.

Start by grabbing a set of waterproof playing cards, and assign a technique to each suit; for example, spades might call for kicking, hearts for drills, diamonds for swimming, and clubs for pulling. Next, assign a distance to groups of numbers (for instance, 2s and 3s might mean 50s, while 4s and 5s might mean 100s, and so on). Keep your jacks, queens, kings, and aces in a separate pile because they’ll dictate the number of repeats (1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively).

So, for example, pulling a 5 of clubs alongside a queen would require you to grab your pull buoy for 2×100. Pulling a 2 of hearts alongside an ace would mean a 5×50 drill.

Another way to bring a measure of unpredictability to your workout is to roll a single die four times to determine your next set. The first roll determines your technique (5s could require kicking), the second your effort level (perhaps 4s always mean sprints), the third your distance (1s could mean 50s), and the fourth your number of reps (anywhere from 1 to 6).

If you were on a summer swim team as a kid, chances are high you played many games of sharks and minnows. The game starts out with one “shark” who tries to tag all the other “minnows” as they swim from one side of the pool to the other. Each swimmer who gets tagged turns into a shark for the next round. You can complicate this game by instituting an underwater safety zone.

If you have an area of the pool to yourself, form teams, set up goals on opposite walls with pull buoys, grab a ball, and play water polo. This is an excellent way to make vertical kicking, sprinting, and treading water more exciting. It also facilitates team bonding.

Head to the deep end for this game to work on endurance as you tread water and practice vertical kicking. If the lifeguards allow it, you can play water volleyball over the flags with an inflatable beach ball. Your pool might even have a water volleyball net, and some versions float so that you can move them as required.

Hopkins recommends “call it sets,” inspired by Bob Steele, to work on pacing and fine-tuning your internal clock. Essentially, you and your training partners will swim a set of 100s, and before each repeat, each one of you will predict the time you expect to hit. Whoever is closest to their estimates wins the set.

Chase sets are a fun way for training groups with seemingly disparate ability levels to unite, says Hopkins. Slower swimmers are allowed a head start, while faster swimmers are tasked with trying to catch them. Chase sets are ideally employed for speedwork, not drills.

Casino night is extraordinarily fun for large teams and helps highlight everyone’s unique talents. First, two or three swimmers who are roughly equivalent in speed line up at the blocks. Then, the other teammates line up behind the swimmer they predict will win.

From there, you’ll use cards or dice to determine the “event” that the swimmers will be competing in (see general rules above in the solo workouts). Whoever has picked the winning swimmer gets a rest break while the rest of the team completes a penalty swim (a 50 sprint, perhaps). If you have one seemingly unbeatable swimmer on the team, you can assign them a permanent handicap.

#8783. Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

Your power meter might be working perfectly, but that doesn’t mean your cycling computer records data accurately. Here’s why you should care and how you can check.

Spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree. Put a power meter on your crank and another on your pedals, and the numbers may not match exactly. That can be frustrating when you’re trying to figure out which one is right, but for most riders, a small, consistent difference isn’t necessarily a problem.

If you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month. Whether your threshold is actually 250 watts or 255 watts matters less than knowing that an interval at that power represents the same effort from one ride to the next.

But what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers? What if the bike computer recording your ride is changing the data before you ever upload it to Strava or TrainingPeaks?

I recently noticed something odd while testing a cycling computer. At first, I was doing this to compare GPS track accuracy, but since I was testing, I also paired all the devices to my heart rate strap and Quarq power meter. When I compared the ride files afterward, what stood out was that their power numbers didn’t match. Initially, the differences were small enough. But when I looked more closely, I noticed it immediately. Every time I stopped pedaling, one computer still recorded power.

Before I get into what the heck sticky watts are, I should say I first learned about the issue in 2025 when I saw a video from Shane Miller, who goes by GPLama on YouTube. The video is called “Power Meter Data Recording: The Wild West?”, and it’s worth watching. Shane was the first person I saw digging into this particular recording issue with cycling computers.

So what the heck is it? Sticky watts happen when a cycling computer keeps recording a power value for a few seconds after you’ve stopped pedaling. Instead of dropping to zero, the last power number gets “stuck” in your ride file until the computer finally catches up.

Let’s say you’re riding along at 250 watts and stop pedaling as you approach a corner. Your computer might continue recording 250 watts for a few seconds while you’re coasting. On a graph, that can look like a flat line extending beyond the point where the power should have dropped.

A few seconds might not sound like much, but think about how often you stop pedaling on a typical ride. Every corner, descent, stop sign, or moment spent coasting in the group is another opportunity for those extra watts to show up in your file. And if you stop pedaling after a hard effort, the computer could be holding a much higher number than 250 watts, which can skew your data.

It’s also worth distinguishing this from the setting on some computers that lets you exclude zeroes when calculating average power. That setting changes how an average is calculated. Sticky watts affect the power values recorded in the ride file itself, so those extra values can still be there when you upload the ride for analysis.

On one ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Garmin Edge 850 and an Edge 1060. The two Garmins recorded almost identical power numbers, but the DURA 2 consistently came out higher. When I looked more closely at the files, I found repeated instances where the COROS continued recording the last power value after both Garmins had dropped to zero.

The difference was especially noticeable during a series of short, hard efforts. After one effort, the DURA 2 recorded 565 watts for four seconds while both Garmins recorded zero. After another, it held 656 watts for three seconds. Across a roughly three-minute section containing several of these efforts, the Garmins averaged about 260 watts, while the COROS recorded nearly 307 watts.

Those short efforts make the issue easy to see, but the difference showed up across the ride, too. In the roughly 98 minutes of matched power data I compared, the DURA 2 averaged about 186 watts, while both Garmins averaged about 179 watts.

On a second ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Hammerhead Karoo, Wahoo ELEMNT ACE, and Garmin Edge 850. Again, the COROS recorded higher power through a section with several hard efforts followed by coasting. The Garmin recorded lower numbers than the Karoo and Wahoo in that section, which reminds us that differences can go both ways when computers record the same power meter.

I was honestly surprised to see this on the DURA 2. The original DURA had similar issues early on, but its power recording improved with subsequent updates, and it performed well in GPLama’s 2025 video presenting the issue. I don’t want to turn this into a story about picking on COROS. The company has a good history of updating and improving its products, and I expect it can address this issue on the DURA 2 as well. For now, these files show why it’s worth paying attention to what your cycling computer records, even when you trust your power meter.

If you mostly ride for fun and don’t pay much attention to your power data afterward, a few extra watts in your ride file probably won’t change your life. But if you use that data to track your training, compare rides, and work with a coach, those differences can matter.

The big problem is that sticky watts don’t necessarily add the same amount to every ride. A steady climb with little coasting might show no difference. But a ride with lots of corners, stop signs, descents, or short, hard efforts followed by coasting could produce a much larger one. That makes it harder to compare rides or judge how much work you actually did.

The easiest way to check is to record the same ride on two cycling computers paired to the same power meter. You don’t necessarily need to buy a second computer. If a friend has one you can borrow, pair both to your power meter and record a ride with a few clear transitions from pedaling to coasting.

Alternatively, you can look closely at the power files your head unit generates. Do a couple of hard efforts, like sprints, where you stop pedaling at the end, then zoom in on those sections. Look for a flat section where one computer continues recording the same power value for several seconds after the other has dropped to zero.

And yes, I know that I’m definitely in some deep weeds over here, and it can be tough to argue that a cycling computer recording a few extra watts is a huge problem worth tackling. For many riders, it might not matter at all. But the current crop of cycling computers is also the most expensive we’ve ever seen. These devices are marketed and sold as precision training tools, and accurate data recording is central to that. These devices should do that, and riders shouldn’t have to question it.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018.
