#8757. How Beginners Can Build Cycling Endurance in Just 3 Days a Week

This coach-backed base training plan helps newer riders improve aerobic fitness, add structure, and make progress with limited time.

Building a base on the bike has traditionally meant putting in a lot of hours doing long, slow distance training. But with work and family lives, it can feel impossible to find the hours in the week to properly commit to a base build, especially if you’re a beginner cyclist who’s not used to rides that take more than three hours.

As it turns out, especially if you’re a newer cyclist, there’s a lot that you can accomplish if you only have three days a week to get on the bike. Building a base of fitness for cycling takes some commitment and consistency, but it doesn’t have to take over your life.

Here, we spoke with Namrita Brooke, Ph.D., one of the lead coaches at BaseCamp, about how she would structure the optimal three-day week on the bike—and what other lifestyle tweaks she would make in order to improve fitness even when you can’t fit in long rides.

A lot of cyclists think that if they can’t train 10-plus hours per week, their fitness will suffer, or they won’t make gains on the bike. This isn’t true, especially for newer riders. “Someone who has not been doing any exercise would see gains in as little as two to four hours a week of riding,” says Brooke. “If someone has some general fitness, gains could be had in four to six hours [per week].”

However, expect that after a few weeks or months, the tangible signs of progress will slow unless you can devote more time to training. “The tricky part is the ongoing gains might not be as easy to see as the initial gains,” Brooke adds. “Initially, if the athlete was measuring power, they would see power increases, but these would plateau in a few months, leading them to think gains are no longer occurring but in reality, the athlete is likely to still build other metrics of fitness like repeatability, durability, and resilience, but those are not as easy to measure.”

Often, new cyclists with limited time tend to attempt one monster ride on the weekend, skipping cycling during the week due to busy lives. But even if you can only eke out two one-hour (or 45-minute!) trainer sessions on weekdays in addition to the long weekend ride, you’ll gain fitness and strength faster than if you stick to a single ride.

“I would rather see the athlete do three quality days a week versus one or even two longer days,” says Brooke.

“The base training goal, whether you’re a pro or average Joe, is to build the best aerobic fitness you can for the training hours you have available,” says Brooke. Without this aerobic fitness, you won’t be able to boost your speed or power on the bike.

This means spending the bulk of your time on the bike in zone 2 (whether you use power, heart rate or perceived exertion). Riding in zone 2—also known as your endurance pace—will mean that you’re able to hold a conversation and speak in full sentences, but it should feel slightly difficult to do so. If you can chat away easily, you’re riding a little too easy. If you’re gasping for air between sentences, you’re riding a little too hard.

By that, we mean your skin. Riding more miles means being aware of skin considerations such as sun protection and chafing prevention. Don’t just ignore reddened skin, use lubricants and padded shorts to feel more comfortable on the bike.

For newer riders, opt for the longer durations in each phase. If you’ve been riding for a while, you’ll likely notice that after a few weeks in each phase, you’re at a point where you’re not noticing any improvements—in that case, proceed to the next phase. Here’s how Brooke would break it down.

2.5-3.5 hours (zone 2), based on how much free time you have available

New riders may need to break up the zone 3 portion of the ride with an easy 5-10 minutes in the middle.

2.5-4 hour (zone 2) based on how much free time you have available

Have an extra hour on Saturday for your long ride? Great! Woke up an hour early on Wednesday and have time to hop on the trainer for an extra 45-minute ride in zone 2? Fantastic. Feel free to add time whenever possible.

Four days on the bike is better than three, says Brooke. “Two harder interval days and two longer days would be best if possible,” she notes. And this is actually a fairly standard schedule for most serious cyclists—they’ll add one or two additional easy rides to the schedule, but the meat and potatoes of their training consists of two longer endurance rides and two harder interval-based sessions.

In fact, Brooke says that often, she hears new cyclists say they only have four hours per week to train, but once they get going, they start to “find” extra time. “You would be surprised how many newer riders think they are limited to four to six hours a week but once they really get into cycling, they make accommodations to squeeze in an extra hour or two per week,” she says. “I see riders all the time start to wake up earlier to squeeze in additional ride time before they start the rest of the day!”

And thanks to the prevalence of indoor trainers, it’s easier than ever to sneak in an extra hour or two on the bike during a weekend or early in the morning, even if you have work or childcare demands on your time. But don’t neglect outdoor riding, especially if your base-building goal is to be able to keep up on the local group ride or jump into a race. While indoor training builds fitness, it doesn’t help improve your skills for riding outdoors, so make time for at least one outdoor ride per week if at all possible.

There is one final caveat: It’s easy to get excited about the prospect of adding a monster ride to your weekend whenever possible, but these long rides aren’t easy. Four hours on the bike will feel very, very different from two hours. If riding for five hours on Saturday means you can barely walk for two days after, or it impacts your training the next week, back off.

Long rides shouldn’t leave you flattened for days afterwards. If they do, you’re doing too much, too soon. And Brooke notes that the longer you ride, the more important it is to properly fuel that long effort!

The fastest way to improve your fitness is—again—by consistently training. But training doesn’t mean all-bike-all-the-time! Brooke says there are quite a few simple additions you can do on those non-cycling days to see gains on the bike.

→ Walk: Often on conference calls for work, or accompanying your kiddos to soccer practice? Walk and talk, or do laps around the field while you cheer. “Walking is more of an aerobic builder than people think and can be a gentle form of aerobic activity to accompany bike time,” Brooke says.

For the office worker, treadmill desks are becoming more popular, and if you do want to put in more bike time and you have a stationary trainer, you can do some easy spinning while answering emails or brainstorming for that big presentation.

→ Strength Train: “Strength training can be added in as little as 15 minutes a day, three days a week if we are willing to change the paradigm of going to the gym and lifting heavy things,” says Brooke. “Integrating just this small amount of functional strength into a base training program like we do at BaseCamp yields long-term benefits to your training and health.”

You can do shortstrength sessions at home with just a couple of weights, or even bodyweight alone to get started.

In a typical training plan, cyclists have three weeks of training followed by a rest week where they do only a couple of shorter, easier rides. When you’re only able to ride three days a week, there’s no reason to take a rest week—you’re already getting plenty of recovery time in the four days you’re off the bike.

“The low training stimulus is likely not enough to elicit a high enough super-compensation response to make the loss of fitness during a rest week worth it,” says Brooke. (That said, if you’re a beginner rider and find that after three weeks, you are feeling fatigued, you can dial down the duration or intensity for that fourth week—but stick to three rides if possible.)

Once you’ve done your base training for several weeks with your rides spread out through the week (i.e Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday), you may want to try switching things up. If you do have the ability to try out new riding days, it’s worth experimenting with doing mini-training blocks, i.e riding three days in a row, some weeks. This subtle shift changes your training stimulus by forcing your body to contend with the need for speedier recovery between rides.

Newer riders may find that it’s harder to recover between rides in these chunks, says Brooke. “The challenge of block training is the athlete needs a certain amount of base fitness to be able to respond and adapt to this type of stimuli and in this scenario,” she explains. “But testing the block process is the only way to find out how they tolerate it.”

If you try riding three days in a row and feel exhausted, go back to your regular schedule and test again after another few weeks of consistent training.

While it’s tempting to stay in the base phase forever, this training phase should really only last around eight weeks. At this point, your aerobic fitness is maximized (for now) and it’s time to focus on the development of “power.”

“After the base phase comes the build phase, where the athlete wants to increase their sustainable max power for a range of times,” says Brooke. “For a newer cyclist without a specific goal, focus on holding a higher wattage for five minutes to 40 minutes. This phase should be maintained as long as the athlete continues to see improvement, then once response begins to fade, move on to the next phases.”

Once you’ve plateaued your power gains, the final phase, typically utilized when “peaking” for an event would be the “speed” phase, explains Brooke. “Here, the cyclist would focus on improving shorter efforts of under five minutes and building anaerobic capacity to focus on performing better in events or group rides.”

After your main event, whether it’s a race or group ride or even just spending four to six weeks focusing on upping your sprint power, it’s time to take a short break and then circle back to base phase.

The good news is that once you’ve completed this cycle, you’ll be pleasantly surprised at how much stronger you’re feeling on the bike the second time you tackle base training. While training phases are cyclical, your fitness grows as you spend more and more time on the bike, so no training phase will feel exactly the same.

Molly writes about cycling, nutrition and training with an emphasis on bringing more women into sport. She's the author of nine books including the Shred Girls series and is the founder of Strong Girl Publishing. She co-hosts The Consummate Athlete Podcast and spends most of her free time biking and running on trails, occasionally joined by her mini-dachshund.

Coach David Lipscomb is the founder of CIS Training Systems, creator of THE SYSTEM 6×6 Framework, and a 1st-degree Black Belt who's spent over three decades helping cyclists of all levels transform their performance through data, discipline, and purpose.

#8756. The Top 11 Women’s Running Shoes That Have the Comfiest Fit, Coziest Cushioning, and Most Responsive Ride

These are the current road and trail favorites of our women’s wear-test team.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 12, 2026: End-of-year sales have already taken off. Our Best Stability Shoe, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25, is now on sale with 19% off. (We are currently testing the newest model, the Adrenaline GTS 26.) Our Best for Speedwork Shoe, the Adidas Adizero Evo SL, is also discounted with 20% off.

We are in a new era of running shoes, from stacked super trainers to plated racers to gravel models decked out with bike-inspired treads.

The industry formerly criticized for “shrink it and pink it,” i.e., the practice of making smaller-size men’s shoes and slapping pink on them and calling them women’s shoes, has gone to great lengths crafting footwear that’s women-specific.

Brands are taking care to produce shoes that accommodate the average woman’s foot shape: wider in the midfoot area, narrower around the heel. But don’t think this list is free of pink shoes. The traditionally feminine colors have been reclaimed by brands like Nike (turns out it’s flashy and easier to spot neon pink Alphaflys). Here you’ll find trainers of every color for all types of women’s feet and women runners.

Shopping for a daily trainer → Brooks Glycerin 23On a budget → New Balance EllipseMostly a run/walker → Hoka Clifton 11On the path to recovery → Hoka Bondi 9Adding in speedwork → Adidas Adizero Evo SLLogging long runs → Nike Vomero 18Racing a marathon → Saucony Endorphin Elite 3An overpronator → Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25Suffering from bunions → Altra Torin 9Running on rail trails → lululemon WildfeelNew to technical terrain → Altra Experience Wild 3

Runner’s World has been around for almost 60 years, providing news, fitness tips, and, of course, gear recommendations for runners. Our product guides for essentials like running shoes and shorts come from our hardworking test team, who put the latest and greatest running gear through their paces day in and day out. These selections come from Senior Reviews Editor Cat Bowen, who blazes the trails and is an ultramarathon beast, and me, Running Reviews Editor Amanda Furrer. I have written about running gear for a decade and hold an even longer Boston Marathon streak, beginning in 2013.

We picked these shoes based on feedback from the runners who are part of our 300-runner-strong team of local wear-testers and the expertise of our editors. We evaluated every shoe over the course of at least 100 miles, paying attention to overall performance, comfort, ride, longevity, and value.

To ensure our shoe recommendations are truly comprehensive and trustworthy, we grabbed a wide array of shoe types to put through our rigorous testing. This involved evaluating them across diverse terrains, including challenging trails, smooth tracks, varied road surfaces, and—of course—treadmills. Our massive wear-test team allows us to gather feedback from individuals ranging from sprinters to marathoners, runners of different weights and body types, those with different foot strikes, shoe needs, and biomechanics. By combining varied surface testing with a diverse runner pool, we learn a ton about each shoe’s performance and suitability for a wide range of users and individual experiences. Based on our extensive testing, the options below are currently the best running shoes for women.

In our testing, we found the Glycerin 23 excelled as a daily trainer over the Ghost 18 among women testers. The formerly max-cushioned Glycerin has evolved into an everyday shoe that you can take out on easy days to long runs. Our women testers preferred the Glycerin 23 over the Ghost 18 because of the shoes’ fit. Several testers reported hot spots in the Ghost 18’s bunion-prone area. The Glycerin 23, on the other hand, was praised for its broad platform, soft and plush knit upper, and ample wiggle room in the toebox.

“The shoe is cushioned in a way that makes me want to do all my long runs in them,” said tester and Senior Features Editor Pavlína Černá. “It doesn’t drag as some cushioned shoes do, but feels responsive. My go-to comparison of a cushioned shoe is the Saucony Echelon which I love for walking/hiking, but which I cannot do long miles in because the shoe drags, makes me work too hard. In comparison, the Glycerin is plushy but responds well to my moods and the corresponding pace changes.”

The shoe has Brooks’s DNA Tuned midsole foam, which was introduced in the even cushier Glycerin Max. The experience running on DNA Tuned is just like Černá described: plush, supportive, responsive, ideal for running long.

One of our women testers described the Ellipse v1 as “nearly perfect.”

New Balance’s intent with the shoe was to provide a high-cushioned, trampoline-like bounce experience for recreation. It’s the kind of shoe you can wear for daily training, while you lace up in it for a casual, conversationally paced group run. The Ellipse was specifically made to make runs easier.

Fresh Foam X is dialed in to produce a foamy, high-rebound ride with reliable shock absorption. It’s a ride that makes me look forward to lacing up the Ellipse and taking it out for whatever kind of run my heart desires on the spot. The tweaked foam makes running in the soft, springy shoe feel like a treat.

“The best word to describe the cushion is plush,” said tester Laura Parks. “It has the extreme cushion sensation of a Hoka Bondi without feeling the weight.” She described the ride as unlike any she’s had running in other Fresh Foam X models.

We’re still in the process of testing the Clifton 11, but the team is already loving the shoe weeks into testing. Everything we love about Hoka—plush cushioning, cozy fit, responsive midsole—is usually encapsulated in each iteration of the Clifton. The 11 is no exception. It was a hard follow after the ClifTEN, but the Clifton 11 makes runs feel effortless, thanks to the compression-molded EVA midsole foam, which provides high rebound and a comfy platform that pillows your foot.

The shoe has Hoka’s Meta-Rocker geometry to promote smooth transitions. Sidewalls make the fit snug but not too narrow as the Hoka Bondi 9.

The Clifton 11 is also excellent for run/walking because of that cushioned support and rocker geometry. These elements make the Clifton reliable at any pace.

The Bondi 9, one of Hoka’s plushest daily trainers, is somehow cushier and sleeker with this update. Hoka added 10 mm to the midsole—but this shoe is no chonk. We even tested it sprinting on the treadmill; the supercritically foamed EVA provides high energy return and soft support. But we especially like using the shoe for run/walking and recovery.

“The Bondi 9 delivers great protection with an amazingly smooth roll,” said tester Tiffany Volpe. “I can see why there is so much hype behind the Hoka and [why it’s called] the Queen of Cushion. I felt like I was sitting down in the midsole. I felt locked in with ample protection especially in the tongue and collar.

“I found the Bondi a perfect recovery day shoe and one that I reach for when I just want to head out for a long slow run to clear my head.”

The shoe was also rated high in stability among testers, and they appreciated the reflective, as well.

Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate boldly dubbed the Adizero Evo SL Shoe of the Year merely a month into 2025. That sentiment is upheld and shared; the shoe is Best Overall on our list of Best Running Shoes. For $150 (and frequently on sale), just above the cost of the New Balance Ellipse, you could also say it’s Best Value. And because of its secret sauce, Adidas’s Lightstrike Pro midsole, which is featured in the brand’s super shoes, you could also say it’s Best for Speedwork, too.

One woman tester gamely raced in the Adizero Evo SL, and experienced excellent results. “The coolest thing about these to me was the weight and cushion,” said that tester, Caroline Lennon. “It was a perfect balance of being light and springy but still feeling well-cushioned and supported. They were so comfortable at all paces and let me feel faster than I was anticipating. They felt best at a harder effort. My 5K race was surprisingly fast given that there was no carbon plate!”

Breaking: A Nike shoe with Hoka-plush cushioning. The Vomero 18 is unlike any Nike we’ve tested. It has a dual-density midsole with 46 mm of ZoomX and ReactX foam, which puts this shoe in the super trainer category. What you get is a bouncy, soft ride that makes long runs an energized quest instead of a Saturday (or Sunday) morning slog.

“I didn’t expect to love this shoe as much as I do!” said Associate Health and Fitness Editor Kristine Kearns, a self-described loyal Brooks Ghost fan. “I wasn’t sure if I would like the Vomero 18 because of how much heel cushioning there is, and how it kind of elevates me forward in that way. But it turns out the shoe provides so much stability, even on the side.”

The source of the stability Kearns is referring to: the wider platform. Nike collected input from women testers, who wanted a wider fit in the midfoot. The result is a more accommodating foot shape that provides midrun support.

The Endorphin Elite 3 makes good with super adjustments after a strong reception with the Endorphin Elite 2. Several testers loved the previous model’s aggressive bounce, becoming inspired to race in it at their next marathon. Others, like me, had difficulty troubleshooting the squishy TPEE foam. It was volatile, pogo stick-like bounce that required mastering before you went all out on this somewhat unstable super shoe.

Saucony tamed the shoe this go-around. That pogo stick bounce is still there, but the ride is more stable with a connected heel and midfoot (not the slightly decoupled heel that made it more likely to turn your foot inward navigating sharp turns). The PwrTrac outsole also adds more support by providing grippy traction.

The Adrenaline GTS 25 is pumped with even more foam for a comfier, more supportive ride. Brooks added 1 mm of DNA Loft v3 foam in the heel and 3 mm in the forefoot, resulting in a slightly higher stack height, lower heel drop, and more responsive ride.

Dense guide rails on the lateral and medial sides of the shoe act as bumpers to help with ankle and knee alignment while running. The support aids overpronators and late-onset overpronators alike.

“One of the shoe’s best features is the sense of security it provides,” said tester Kylie Rodriguez. “The Adrenaline series is known for its stability, and this model is no exception. I felt confident and secure on every surface, from slick sidewalks to uneven dirt paths.

“This blend of comfort, stability, and a lightweight feel makes the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 a fantastic and reliable choice for any runner looking for a do-it-all shoe. It’s a solid, dependable performer that won’t let you down. Another solid key component to the shoe was the cupping support the heel gave my strong heel striking steps even more confidence and support.”

We’re still getting in Torin 9 feedback, but it’s safe to say early on that the shoe is a worthy follow-up to the Torin 8. When Altra was founded in 2009, its core values were balanced zero-drop cushioning, an accommodating toebox for toe-splaying, and a women-specific fit. The brand has evolved with a 4mm-drop shoe line but its values haven’t changed.

The Torin, basically the Ghost version of a zero-drop shoe, is a terrific cushioned entry into running a no-drop shoe. Dual-density foam provides a moderate but supportive bed of cushioning to help you transition into zero-drop running. Runners with wide feet and bunions will also appreciate Altra’s wide toebox, which not only allows your toes to wiggle but also helps with your biomechanics (squeezed toes help you run faster, said no one ever).

The updated outsole is Vibram XS Dura, which is grippier than the rubber on the Torin 8. I like how the shoe can dabble off road and not have to worry about falling face-first when I traverse onto a trail—which is rare.

The lululemon shoe team has made it its mission to produce women-specific trainers since the release of the brand’s first running shoe, the Blissfeel, in 2022. Their latest model, the Wildfeel, provides the same comfy, secure fit with a responsive, high-rebound ride off-road.

The shoe has men’s and women’s editions, which are tweaked to support each sex’s anatomical differences and distinct biomechanics. For instance, the forefoot of the women’s shoe is slightly more flexible than the men’s to complement the shorter toes, longer arch, and shorter instep typical of women’s feet.

Our testers appreciated the Wildfeel’s flexibility and overall comfort. It’s a good choice for runners new to the trail who want more of a hybrid option that can take on some technical track.

“I loved the flexibility of the Wildfeels!” said tester Jenny Stump. “I am primarily a road runner. These felt comfortable enough that I could do some easy miles on the road as well as tackle some trails with uneven surfaces. All the trail runners I have previously tried felt more stiff and had such a thick sole that I wouldn’t even want to warm up on the road with them.”

What I love most about the Experience Wild 3 is that it’s a trail shoe that feels like a road shoe. The fit is accommodating in the midfoot and toe area—Altra is known for its spacious toeboxes that allow your toes to splay—and the collar and tongue are padded and cushioned.

The Altra Ego P35 foam is responsive on the trail and provides a nice balance of support and ground feel. Another win for me, the mostly road runner: the shoe is incredibly flexible. No stiffness or hot spots that cause my feet a world of hurt the first couple of runs before they’re broken in.

The shoes have gaiter attachments to provide even more protection and a toe sweep. The drop is a low 4 mm, which isn’t as intimidating as going full zero (though if you’re game, the Lone Peak 9 is a good place to start).

The shoe is also available as the Experience Wild 3+, which has a Vibram Megagrip outsole. It’s a little more expensive at $165. If you want tackier grip, go for it. But the 3.5mm lugs on the MaxTrac outsole suit me and fellow testers just fine on slush, mud, and icy snow.

Women’s feet have distinct structural differences than men’s feet. From shape to proportions to biomechanics, all of these things significantly impact shoe fit and comfort. For example, while men’s feet typically present a more uniform width from heel to forefoot, women’s feet tend to be wider in the forefoot relative to the heel. Any lady who has felt their toes get squished as their heel slips right out of the shoe knows this issue.

Recognizing these anatomical differences, and responding to the hoards of women runners clamoring for something better, running shoe manufacturers have (finally) started to incorporate more gender-specific design elements into their products. This means crafting shoes with distinct features tailored to the unique shape and biomechanics of women’s feet. For instance, a women’s running shoe might feature a wider toebox to accommodate the broader ball of the foot, while a narrower heel counter secures the back of the foot and prevents slippage.

Additionally, the materials used in the heel construction might differ between men’s and women’s versions to account for variations in where we strike our foot when we land. Women and men obviously have different centers of gravity—especially when we’re pregnant—and that changes how we strike and the wear pattern of our soles.

Brands are not just shrinking and pinking the shoes anymore. Their aim is to enhance performance and prevent running-related aches and pains. A shoe that fits properly and supports the foot’s natural movement can improve running efficiency and reduce the risk of common running-related injuries, such as blisters, plantar fasciitis, the pedi-ick black toenails, and shin splints.

Researchers have also found that, because women tend to have wider hips than men, women’s feet are more likely to strike the ground toward the outside of their shoe soles. The inward rolling of the foot, called pronation, that results from this explains why more women are believed to overpronate than men (aka, walk a bit duck-footed.). Some women’s running shoes account for this increased tendency with stability features in the sole, such as guide rails and medial posts, to provide more support.

This list includes what we regard as the best shoe in its category. But there are still plenty of other shoes for you to choose from.

For the plushest ride and more foam underfoot, check out the Best Cushioned Running Shoes.

If you’re an overpronator or think you need more support, take a look at the Best Stability Shoes.

And if you want more of a selection of non-road shoes, visit the Best Trail Shoes.

No matter the distance or your shoe preferences, there’s a great shoe for you on our lists.

What’s the size difference between men’s and women’s running shoes?

If you prefer wearing men’s running shoes, size down 1.5. For example: A women’s size 10 would equal a men’s size 8.5.

When should you change out your running shoes?

Running shoe shelf life is dependent on the runner. Some runners wear down their shoes after only a couple weeks, others have their shoes well past several months. The standard mileage on everyday trainers is 350 to 500 miles, 250 to 300 for lightweight shoes, and 100 to 250 for racing or minimalist shoes.

If you don’t keep track of mileage, a good rule of thumb is switching out shoes twice a year. For racing shoes, two to three races.

You can put your shoes in the washing machine with some detergent, set on cold. Never put your shoes in the dryer—it will melt the glue and make them degrade faster.

Instead, remove the insoles and allow them to air dry. Stuff wads of newspaper inside your shoes and leave them to sit for a couple hours so the paper can absorb the moisture.

#8755. Best Winter Cycling Gloves for Cold, Wet, and Windy Rides

We rode through freezing rain, sleet, and biting wind to find the best winter cycling gloves that stay warm, dry, and secure when conditions are at their worst.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Nothing ruins a chilly, crisp day on the bike faster than frozen fingers. Besides being uncomfortable, numb hands can make it difficult to shift gears or feel your brake levers, turning a cold ride into a potentially unsafe one.

The right pair of winter gloves will keep your hands warm without making it difficult to operate your bike’s controls. But finding that pair isn’t always as simple as checking the temperature rating on the packaging. How warm your hands get, the weather conditions, and the type of riding you do all play a role.

For example, on a 35-degree road ride, you’ll likely want a much warmer glove than you would for a mountain bike ride at the same temperature. Higher speeds on the road mean more windchill, while a slower, harder effort on the trails can leave your hands sweaty in gloves that are too warm. If you ride throughout the winter, it’s worth owning a few different pairs to cover the range of conditions you’ll encounter.

I tested more than 40 glove models in temperatures ranging from the low 60s to below 20 degrees, then narrowed the field to my six favorites. I’ve included recommended temperature ranges for each, but consider those a starting point. If you tend to run cold or have Raynaud’s syndrome, you may want a warmer glove; if your hands sweat easily, a lighter, more breathable option might work better.

More Winter Gear Advice: Our Expert Swears by This Three-Layer Trick. ● The Best Men’s Winter Cycling Jackets ● The Best Winter Cycling Hats

Perhaps my all-time favorite version of my all-time favorite glove, DeFeet’s Duraglove has been around for ages and has remained mostly unchanged. It’s very comfortable, has great dexterity, and provides good grip. Plus, it has touchscreen functionality. DeFeet offers two versions of this glove: The plain Duraglove ET and the Duraglove ET Wool Blend featured here, which uses a merino wool blend.

I’ve found this version to be the warmer of the two. I’ve worn this glove into the low 40s during high-intensity rides and stayed comfortable. Because this knit glove is incredibly breathable, it’s still comfortable to wear as the day warms into the mid-to-high 50s. The Duraglove is unsuitable for rainy rides as its knit construction will quickly soak up water.

These Assos gloves feel like they shouldn’t be as warm as they are. But don’t let their thin, stretchy, low-bulk material fool you. These gloves have kept my hands toasty and comfortable into the high 30s, and I have mountain biked in them at near-freezing temperatures with no issues.

They use soft fleece fabric inside and have an outer layer with excellent wind resistance. Assos also applies a water-repellent treatment to manage light rain and spray from damp roads. I’m a big fan of the palm of these gloves. They feature very minimal padding that helps with grip and bar feel. Fit and construction are excellent, with long cuffs to keep cold air out of your jacket, plus touchscreen functionality that works very well. The only knock against these gloves is their price. However, my personal pair is now in its fourth winter with no signs of wear, making these an easy recommendation if you want a good pair of gloves that will last.

Near-freezing temperatures with rain are probably the most challenging conditions to ride in. But for some, it’s unavoidable. Glacier Glove’s Ice Bay is as good as it gets for these conditions. It’s constructed with 2mm-thick, fleece-lined neoprene and is as waterproof as any piece of clothing could be.

These gloves have incredible dexterity given their warmth. The long cuff is easy to tuck under your rain jacket to keep water out. The downside of a neoprene glove is that it does not breathe at all. That’s partly how it keeps your hands warm, but it only works as long as you keep the gloves on. If you take them off, your now-sweaty hands will get quite cold quickly, and your formerly toasty gloves (lacking body heat) will be cold and wet with sweat. Despite these drawbacks, if it’s cold and rainy and I need to be out riding, these are the gloves I reach for.

These pricey gloves are the warmest five-finger gloves I’ve tried that still let me move my fingers. Gore took inspiration from high alpine mountaineering for the design. The outer shell uses a Gore-Tex ePE liner that is highly wind- and water-resistant. For insulation, Gore used a PrimaLoft lining. It features one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios. All of this results in a glove that can be comfortable down to and below freezing, depending on your pace and specific riding conditions.

I’ve used similarly warm gloves from other brands, and they've often been far too bulky to feel useful. These still maintain a good bar feel and let me freely articulate my fingers. While they have touchscreen compatibility, I found them a little too bulky to quickly type out a text message on an iPhone.

We’ve been using Pearl Izumi’s AmFIB Lobster Gloves for more than a decade. And they’re still one of the best gloves for when temps plummet.

The gloves are made with 170g PrimaLoft Gold insulation, AmFIB soft-shell polyester-polyurethane fabric, and Ax Suede Laredo synthetic leather. It has the kind of exceptional warmth you’d get in a mitten. Yet the AmFIBs still allow for ample dexterity so you can operate both your shifters and brake levers. There’s also a gel palm pad for comfort while gripping the handlebar, plus touchscreen compatibility for the index finger and thumb.

The secret to the dexterity is the PrimaLoft Gold insulation, which provides exceptional warmth without adding bulk. Most very warm gloves are also very thick, which makes it difficult to locate the proper shifter and grip your brake levers. This pair keeps my hands warm on long weekend rides and daily commutes, even when temperatures dip below freezing, without getting in the way.

Bar Mitts may look unconventional, but riders who use them swear by their added warmth and control. Designed to work with gloves, these neoprene covers attach to your bar and enclose your bike’s shifters and brake levers. They add significant wind protection and help keep your hands shielded from the elements.

Several Bar Mitt variants are available for road, mountain, and townie-style handlebars. Be sure to check details and confirm fitment with your bar/shifter combo before you order.

Glove fit is subjective. They should fit in the Goldilocks range. If your gloves are too big, you risk losing grip on the handlebar and controls. But a glove that’s too tight can prevent you from comfortably grasping the handlebar or grips.

An easy way to spot a glove that’s too big is if you have a lot of fabric bunching in your palm. It’s always worth trying new gloves on your bike to see how they feel on the bars, since labeled sizing can differ from brand to brand.

If you’re riding in temperatures below the mid-40s or closer to freezing, you want a glove with some insulation. In the most basic definition, insulation is filling used to capture and hold onto warmth. The most familiar insulation for outdoor use is down, often found in puffy jackets. In gloves, you are most likely to find down in very bulky mittens, which are very warm but lack the dexterity for cycling.

Most cycling-specific gloves use synthetic insulation from companies like Polartech or PrimaLoft. These materials are most often used on the back of the hand to protect from wind and minimize interference with the handlebar feel. Thin, grippy material is generally found on the palm. Many brands use leather on the palms for improved grip and durability, so watch out for this if you avoid buying animal products.

For the interior of the glove, look for polyester or Merino wool. You want something that wicks sweat and keeps your hands dry—sweaty hands can quickly turn into frozen prunes.

Gloves with appropriate breathability for the temperature and your riding effort keep your hands warm and dry. The warmer the temps, or the higher your effort, the more breathable you’ll want your gloves.

Regionally, humidity also plays a part in selecting the right glove. If you ride somewhere cool and dry, such as Colorado, where it might be in the 30s with low humidity, you likely will be able to use a lighter pair of more breathable gloves. These can do a much better job keeping you warm because they transfer moisture away from your hands more effectively. If you ride in the Northeast, the same pair of gloves might feel too cold at the same temperature, since humidity is often much higher. For these conditions, you’ll want a glove with better wind and waterproofing at the expense of breathability.

Once you figure out the glove warmth you need for your riding, consider other features before buying. Something I find very important in gloves meant for frigid weather is long cuffs. Cuffs make it easy to tuck the glove under or sometimes over your jacket sleeve, keeping your wrists warm and stopping cold air from entering your jacket.

The palm construction of a glove is also worth careful examination. A common feature is padding. Some riders prefer padded gloves, while others do not. Padding matters less the warmer a glove gets, since the palm becomes bulkier with insulation. For thinner gloves, a seamless palm is the way to go. It minimizes any chance of irritation and improves handlebar feel.

If you ride with a smartphone or have a touchscreen computer, gloves that interact with these devices are great. The less you need to remove your gloves in the cold, the happier your hands will be.

Finally, a soft, large terrycloth nose-wipe section (preferably along the thumb or index finger) is good if you’re a heavy snotter.

#8754. 6 Budget Running Watches That Deliver Accurate GPS, Long Battery Life, and Much More

Not-so-average watches for the average runner.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

I’ve spent the last several years testing running watches, from the $800 flagships with topographical maps and training-readiness scores to the ones that do almost nothing except tell you how fast you’re going. Both have their place.

“Basic” has become an insult, and I’d like us to cut that right the heck out. A basic running watch isn’t a cheap, crappy watch—it’s a watch that does what it was meant for. Pace, distance, splits, a lap button you can hit with sweaty or frozen fingers, a battery that won’t quit at mile 20, and a screen you can read no matter how tired. That’s the job. These do the job.

They’re also—and this surprises people—what a lot of very fast runners wear. Stand near the front of a starting corral sometime and count the watches that cost less than the shoes. Elites don’t need a wrist device to tell them they’re tired. They need accurate splits.

If you’re new, that’s the biggest thing you need. Nothing kills a running habit faster than forty metrics you don’t understand that insist you’re doing it wrong. Same goes if you’re kitting out a kid for their first track or cross-country season: buy the simple device. It’ll survive the school bus, the mud, and the whole season. And they’ll learn to run by feel, which is the entire point. My first Garmin was essentially a pace-watching brick on my wrist and I still managed PRs. Here’s what I’d actually put on your wrist.

Our Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate tested the Pace 4 and came away calling it a fast, accurate, lightweight GPS watch that nails the basics without charging laptop-level prices. The Coros Pace 4 adds a sharp, always-on AMOLED display and significantly improved battery life over the Pace 3, offering up to 31 hours in max GPS mode (about 24 with the screen always on), all while keeping the case compact and comfortable on the wrist.

It tracks advanced run-specific metrics like running power, ground contact time, and left/right strength balance: That might not be necessary for new and casual runners, but they are useful measurements for training. (There’s a reason why RW Senior Reviews Editor Cat Bowen named it “Best Value” in our overall Best Running Watches guide.)

GPS performance is a standout, with dual-frequency technology delivering smooth, reliable tracks even in neighborhoods and city environments that can throw cheaper chips off course. Dengate also highlights the new voice log feature, which lets you record post-run thoughts that automatically transcribe into the Coros app, making training logs easier to maintain.

At 40 grams with the silicone band (32 grams with nylon), the watch feels barely there in daily use and workouts, though Dengate dislikes the finicky digital dial—especially with gloves—and finds notification text too small to read easily mid-run. For runners who value turn-by-turn, full-color maps, the Pace 4’s breadcrumb-only navigation may be a limitation, but for most no-frills runners wanting accurate tracking, solid battery life, and a modern screen at an entry-level price, it is a compelling choice.

Look, I’ve spent more money on a pair of running shoes than this watch costs. And, honestly? That’s a little embarrassing for the shoes. At $170, the Amazfit Active 3 Premium is wildly outperforming its price tag, and in the words of Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate, if you can find better (for the price) I’ll eat it.

For new runners, this watch is a gift. There’s a whole training library that walks you through what a tempo run or a fartlek actually is, instead of assuming you already know. You get pace, cadence, heart rate zones, running power, and form metrics like ground contact time, which is stuff I did not have on watches costing three times as much. It also has free offline maps with turn-by-turn navigation, so you can leave your phone in your pocket. The cheapest Garmin with offline mapping is over $700.

The recovery metrics are right up there with Garmin and Apple: Training load, VO2 Max, readiness recommendations, sleep and HRV tracking that’s detailed enough to make you rethink that 5 p.m. Diet Coke. It nudges you toward rest days with a little less guilt than Garmin.

The nitpicks: The user experience needs polish—do not disturb is fiddlier than it should be, and the four buttons are sensitive. I’ve paused mid-run more than once with an errant sleeve. Still, for the money? Nothing touches it.

At just around $300, the Polar Pacer has some great training specific features that make it especially useful for competitive runners training on a budget.

Its built-in running program can help you create a training plan to get ready for a 5K, 10K, half marathon, or marathon. Using the Polar Flow app, you can select your race type and date (or the name of the race) and it will create specific workouts to follow within the app that are synched to your watch to follow along. It also provides comprehensive training insights after intervals and long runs, and tracks your long-term fitness trends outside of training.

There are also niche, but useful features like fueling and hydration reminders, and “Training Load Pro,” which monitors strain and recovery. As someone who isn’t great at taking cues from my body when it’s time to take a break, having an active reminder was helpful. (And something you can usually expect in an affordable running watch.)

Although I generally liked Polar’s hardware and software design, I felt that Polar could have used the space of its 1.2-inch MIP display a bit more effectively. Much of the text was small, and the screen had lots of unnecessary white space that could have been used to support more specs, or at least a larger font.

I also found it a bit unintuitive that the “red” button was used for intervals, rather than a start/stop button. It ended up working out great–it’s a helpful button–but there was a bit of a learning curve.

For race runners who want support to help them train, but may not be able to afford a coach or training program, the Pacer feels about as close to having a coach on your wrist as possible at this price point.

The Garmin Forerunner 70 is Garmin’s new entry-level running watch, priced at $250, and it’s a great pick for beginners.

It has a 1.2-inch AMOLED touchscreen, which is the same panel tech found on watches costing twice as much, so it looks and feels more premium than you’d expect at this price. More importantly, it includes Training Readiness and Training Status, features that used to be reserved for watches costing $400 or more, plus an on-device Quick Workouts generator and free Garmin Coach plans for 5K, 10K, and half-marathon training—no subscription needed.

The five buttons make it easy to navigate menus, and it’s light and comfortable for daily wear. Battery life is boss too: they say it’s up to 13 days in smartwatch mode and 23 hours in GPS mode, but in real life? You’re getting a full week. It skips extras like multi-band GPS and NFC payments, but for a new runner focused on building a habit and understanding their training, that’s an easy trade.

Before I switched to a “proper” running watch, I started my wearable tech journey by tracking runs on an Apple Watch. I trained for my first marathon using one, and I actually still wear an Apple Watch SE between runs because of its effective multi-sport fitness tracking and quality of life features like setting voice-activated timers.

Though the Apple Watch is generally beloved, we generally steer runners towards brands like Garmin and Coros, which offer more robust tracking features and better battery life, often at lower prices than Apple’s generalist counterparts. That said, Apple Watches still work well for casual runners, tracking the basics and giving you lifestyle features that you won’t find on other watches in this price range.

To keep it to $300 with GPS and cellular, we recommend the smaller of the SE’s two sizes, 40mm, which translates to a 1.57-inch display. (The larger 44mm version starts at $280 without cellular, though you can sometimes find it for less.) Both versions are far larger than any of my other basic recommendations, which is great if you have a larger wrist or need a large screen for visibility. I personally like the smaller version, which keeps the watch light but still easy to read.

Apple Watches also generally feature a wider range of wrist band options, first- and third-party, and the SE’s bands come in two sizes: If comfort has been an issue for you, this watch gives you the best chance of finding something that feels good.

Apple offers two related apps that utilize your run data–the fitness focused Apple Fitness and the more metrics-minded Apple Health. Fitness allows you to create workouts and segments for training, while charting deep metrics. You can see a lot of information at a glance, too, including time elapsed, heart rate, rolling mile (pace over the last mile), average pace, and distance. That said, I didn’t love the way Apple organized my workout data, you need to search by date rather than just checking an activity log. (Of course, you can always switch to Strava or Nike Run Club if you don’t like the system.)

If you have a child who is starting to exercise and wants to track their steps like mom and dad, the Garmin Bounce is a special smartwatch designed for kids that covers basic fitness tracking and serves as a controlled way for parents to keep tabs, both via texting and GPS tracking.

The Bounce is designed for kids, which is to say that it’s built to withstand them. It’s durable and water-resistant with an IP68 rating, so it can go anywhere with them. The battery lasts up to two days, minimizing the chance that it’ll run dry on them. It also has a colorful UI that encourages kids to engage with the watch and their metrics, and activities and games to help get them moving.

In terms of tracking, the Bounce falls short of my usual standards for tracking: It just shows time and distance. For a kid–not a teen or even a tween, but a kid–that’s about as much as they can handle or care about. That data syncs with the Garmin Jr. app, which parents can access remotely.

It’s worth noting that both the parenting and games features have elements that require mobile WiFi (LTE) support, so you will likely want to add it to your mobile data plan, which will add about $10/month to your monthly bill.

Overall, this is a great way to help kids start to move around more and start thinking about the concept of exercise.

Every watch on this list costs $300 or less. That’s the line I drew, and I drew it on purpose: you shouldn’t have to spend a car payment to find out whether you like running.

I’ve spent my running career strapping these things to my wrist—testing, logging miles, and digging through what’s actually worth buying right now. What made the cut are watches that nail the fundamentals: speed, heart rate, and location, tracked with reasonable accuracy. (If the gap between 155 and 156 bpm matters to you, you need a pricier watch or, better yet, a dedicated HRM. For everyone else, this is plenty.) From there, they earn their spots with battery life that won’t leave you hunting for a charger, multi-sport modes, advanced biometrics like blood oxygen, and built-in coaching programs.

Here’s the part nobody says out loud: a basic watch is the best way to figure out what you actually want. It shows you real data, real proof that the hard work is working. And by the time you’re ready to shell out for something flashier, you’ll know exactly which features you really need.

At the bare minimum, an affordable running watch needs to track your pace, heart rate, route, distance, and time—with at least moderate precision, and displayed in a way you can read at mile 9 when your eyes are glazing over. It should have GPS, so you can map your routes and find your way home, and it should be accurate.

But basic doesn’t mean bare-bones. Plenty of watches in this range monitor more nuanced heart rate data, like your body’s ability to use oxygen during exercise (VO2 max). Most throw in sleep tracking and multi-sport modes, and many will synthesize your training data into insights that can help you get faster.

Spend more and you’ll get mid-tier and high-end watches with features that are nice to have but almost never essential: bigger and more precise sensors, LTE and WiFi support, contactless payment, onboard music storage. Worth knowing: some of the most elite runners in the world train and race in shockingly basic watches. The watch doesn’t run the miles. You do.

Checking your stats mid-run on a sunny day is miserable if the display is small and dim. The best running watches use an AMOLED display which is the same tech found in high-end smartphones and it has brighter colors and deeper contrast, so your numbers stay legible in full daylight.

An AMOLED screen isn’t a guarantee at $250, but that doesn’t mean you’re stuck squinting. Several watches I recommend use a transflective Memory-in-Pixel (MIP) display, which trades vibrant color for battery efficiency and stays highly visible outdoors. Pixel density matters just as much as the panel type, as does maximum brightness, measured in nits.

Most running watches have an auto-off backlight to conserve battery, but the screen should snap on the instant you raise your arm. You should never be standing there waiting for your own watch.

Size-wise, basic running watches run small. They’re roughly 1 to 1.6 inches. A bigger screen makes it easier to see your route map and stats, and gives you room to fit more data on screen if you customize your workout display.

Every smartwatch brand makes a companion app for iOS and Android that stores and analyzes your run data. Because the watch display is tiny, your phone is almost always the better place to adjust settings, rearrange screens, and build workouts.

If you have an iPhone, you already know Apple Fitness. Garmin, Coros, and Polar all offer companion apps with similar functionality, though some are meaningfully easier to live with than others. And any running watch worth buying should support the big third-party apps like Strava and Runna.

Aside from Apple’s watches, even the budget-friendly models I recommend only need charging every week or so, and they juice back up fast. The best of the best go over a fortnight on a single charge.

Keep your expectations calibrated, though: manufacturer battery estimates are best-case scenarios, and your watch probably won’t hit them. Real-world battery life varies charge to charge, and your mileage depends on, well, your mileage. Continuous GPS tracking during workouts is the biggest drain by far. You can switch features off to stretch the time between charges, but a good watch gives you plenty of run time either way.

A good running watch should feel light enough that you forget it’s there. At this price you rarely find something heavy and bulky, but check how it sits on your wrist before you take it out for miles. Some of my picks come in multiple sizes, which helps if you have smaller or larger wrists.

Make sure the band is highly adjustable and can feel secure without being too tight. And remember that many watch bands are replaceable, so if the stock strap isn’t working for you—comfort-wise or style-wise—you have options.

Known as a “social network for athletes,” Strava has become increasingly popular since its launch in 2009. By connecting your running watch to the app, you can upload your runs to the platform for your “friends” to see and give each other “kudos”. The app also tracks PR for different distances and frequent segments that you can get badges for.

It can be an easy way for you to keep all your running data in the same place, especially if you’re using different brands of running watches to track your runs. Plus, you can unlock more features, such as advanced training metrics, with the full paid membership.

What heart rate do I need to hit to get faster?

According to Mayo Clinic, runners should aim for a target heart rate zone of 70- to 85 percent of their maximum heart rate to improve speed over time. This is also known as Zone 2, which some runners tout as the ultimate training metric. A running watch can help you figure out your max heart rate and will allow you to monitor your heart rate during and after the run.

Do basic running watches track distance and heart rate accurately?

For both mapping and logging distance, smartwatches rely on a Global Position System (GPS), which uses satellites to precisely track your location. The quality of your specific watch’s tracking can vary, both based on the quality of the GPS system and on environmental factors like tall buildings and crowds.

That said, the quality of GPS tracking in smartwatches is quite high across the board: Nothing’s perfect, but you can expect your location to be accurate to within a few feet, and your movement to be captured precisely.

Running watches are set to connect with US GPS systems, but you can also opt to connect with other systems like Galileo (European Union) and GLONASS (Russia) to try to improve your accuracy, something I recommend for those experiencing disruptions.

For heart rate, smartwatches rely on optical heart rate sensors that use light (those green beams coming out of the bottom of your watch) to measure blood flow changes in the skin's capillaries and determine your heart rate. They are fairly accurate, generally to within a few beats per minute (BPM). That said, a dedicated heart rate monitor that you strap to your chest will generally provide more accurate readings.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

#8753. Isakova and Hidalgo Win Final WTCS Races in Abu Dhabi, Jorgensen Podiums

The postponed WTCS Abu Dhabi brought the World Triathlon Championship Series, as it is currently known, to a close ahead of its transition to T50 racing within the Triathlon World Tour. The sprint-distance showdown still attracted many of the sport’s top names, with Olympic qualification points and the chance to finish the season on a high and build momentum into 2027.

The top spot on the podium was wide open in the women’s race, with the series’ undefeated champion Cassandre Beaugrand (FRA) absent. Add to the mix the shorter, sprint-distance format and hot, windy conditions set to play a factor, and it was anyone’s guess who would take it.

2025 world champion Lisa Tertsch (GER) was the big name going in, alongside Jeanne Lehair (LUX), who had been part of a sprint finish at the World Cup in Hong Kong the week before. However, Diana Isakova (RUS) was another athlete many had their eyes on after winning that sprint against Lehair and taking the World Cup win in Rome before that. American Gwen Jorgensen (USA) had shown glimmers of top form in recent races, placing fifth at WTCS Weihai and producing the second-fastest run split at the Grand Final in Pontevedra.

Into the warm, 82-degree water, three groups began to form near the front as the chop and currents made for one of the most difficult swims of the year.

Isakova and Lehair were among the first group out of the water, while Tertsch and Jorgensen exited more than 20 seconds behind. That deficit would quickly balloon to over 30 seconds early on the bike, with another group between them and the front of the race.

Halfway through the bike, the front group of nine maintained its advantage as the third group swallowed the second to form one large chase pack. On such a tight, technical course, the larger group offered little additional benefit as the smaller pack ahead steadily increased its lead.

At the end of the bike, Germany’s Laura Lindemann (GER) almost undid the work of the front, mishandling her bike after the dismount, almost causing a crash. Onto the run, a quick transition shot Isakova to the front, while around 36 seconds behind, Jorgensen and Tertsch were among the large group with significant work to do – and only 5km to do it.

By halfway, Isakova and Lehair were clear at the front, foreshadowing a repeat of the race in Hong Kong the week prior. Jorgensen remained 36 seconds behind but had gapped Tertsch and made her way into eighth place.

That momentum continued for Jorgensen as suddenly eighth place became third and she could see the leaders up ahead. Unfortunately, the gap was just too large at that point. Isakova made her move with over 200 meters to go, picking up her first WTCS win and cementing her remarkable end to the year.

Lehair finished second and reflected that her efforts on the bike may have affected her run: “I may have used too much energy, but I am super happy with second place and my third podium of the year.”

Jorgensen couldn’t believe her result, returning to the WTCS podium for the first time since 2016 at 40 years old and producing the fastest run split of the day.

“I thought I was out of this race but one of the coaches told me I was third and I couldn’t believe it,” she shared.

In the men’s race, this year’s Grand Final winner and sprint-distance specialist Matt Hauser (AUS) was wearing bib #1. With his prowess in the water, all eyes were on him in the absence of new world champion Vasco Vilaça (POR). Brazil’s Miguel Hidalgo (BRA), meanwhile, was looking to finally turn his training form into a result after some disappointing recent outings.

New Zealand’s Hayden Wilde (NZL) was the other big name on the lineup, having recently been approved to race both WTCS Abu Dhabi and Dubai T100. With the races falling within 24 hours of each other, that would not normally be allowed under World Triathlon rules. With his eyes firmly back on the Olympics, this was Wilde’s A-race for the weekend, according to New Zealand’s National Performance Manager Stephen Sheldrake.

It started with a windy, choppy swim that mostly stayed compact until the return to the beach, when two lines formed toward the shore. One group, including Hauser, made a beeline for the beach to get out of the water as soon as possible and run along the shore toward transition. That worked well for the Australian, who entered T1 with a small gap over compatriot Luke Willian (AUS).

Wilde found himself 39 seconds in arrears, with work to do alongside recent Iquique World Cup winner David Cantero del Campo (ESP). They were in a large chase group aiming to gain time on the lead group of 11, but on such a short, fast, five-lap bike course, their work was cut out for them.

Almost immediately, however, the gap was nearly cut in half, with Wilde driving the chase to within 22 seconds by the end of the first lap. The pace was so hot that the group split apart, with only a few athletes able to go with him on the technical course.

Perhaps that woke up the front group, which managed to limit its losses over the remainder of the bike and reached T2 with around nine seconds on Wilde and company. It was less than they would have hoped for against the stellar Kiwi runner, but the big question was whether the bike had stung his legs enough to hold him off. A slow transition from the 2025 winner of this race gave him even more work to do.

Onto the run, it didn’t take long for Hauser and Hidalgo to separate themselves at the front. Behind them, Wilde quickly recovered from his transition losses and moved through the rest of the front group alongside Shachar Sagiv (ISR).

The front two continued to push the pace and began adding time to Wilde behind. Hidalgo made his move before the second lap, and Hauser wasn’t able to respond. He quickly began to lose ground as the Brazilian looked comfortable all the way to the finish, taking the tape with an unmatched 14:20 5km.

It was a much-needed WTCS win to carry momentum into the 2027 Triathlon World Tour. Hauser shared afterward that he “could really feel the legs – and the whole year – in the back end of that race.”

Wilde crossed the line in third, comfortably ahead of the rest of the field, but a 14:52 5km left him short of the run speed he is accustomed to producing in these races. He won’t have much time to digest the result, however, as he immediately has to travel to Dubai, where he would look to continue his undefeated T100 season.

#8751. ‘At 60, I Went From Zero Running Experience to Finishing the NYC Marathon Within a Year. These 5 Strategies Got Me to the Finish.’

A first-time marathoner over 50 shares the training, mindset, and support that carried him 26.2 miles.

I’ve never been a runner. Before this past year, the last time I ran was a local 5K on a whim with my daughter about a decade ago. I didn’t prepare for it at all, so it was challenging, and I never ran again after that.

Then, this past May, I signed up to run another local 5K, two months before I turned 60. Working in an office full of runners—I’m an editor at Popular Mechanics and we share an office with Runner’s World—I just wanted to prove that I could do it.

I went on a handful of runs before the race in an attempt to prepare, but I couldn't really make it past 1.5 miles. I got really frustrated. Leading up to race day, I saw how hilly the course was and decided to just wing it. If I had to walk at some points, I’d walk… and that’s what I did on most hills, because I didn’t quite have the stamina to make it through.

But all the runners around me were so inspiring; it felt like we could all make it through together. I saw someone in front of me going about the same pace, and that helped pull me to the finish line. I finished in 35:16, averaging an 11:20 pace.

A few months later, I got the opportunity to run the New York City Marathon. I was hesitant to accept, because I didn’t think I could run that far, but a few of my colleagues pushed me to say yes and really believed in me. So I signed up.

GET YOUR ZERO-TO-MARATHON TRAINING PLAN HERE

When I started marathon training, I followed the Runner’s World six-month zero-to-marathon training plan. I skipped a few weeks ahead because I had already worked up to running five miles and the plan starts with walking.

My training experience was far from perfect, but I learned that as a beginner, you have to just start and go from there.

To be totally honest, I didn’t train for the marathon as much as I probably should have. I started training around early August by running three times a week on local trails in the evenings, averaging three- to five-mile easy runs. I also made sure to add hills to most of my runs to get my quads ready for the hills in New York.

My training came to a bit of a halt after the first few weeks of training, when I realized I probably needed to contact my cardiologist. A couple of years ago, the doctors told me I have an enlarged aorta (the largest artery in your body that carries blood from your heart to the rest of your body), which the doctor attributed to my physically demanding years as an ironworker.

The problem with an enlarged aorta is that if it ruptures, you could have a fatal heart attack with little to no warning signs. Thinking about this made me nervous to train out of fear I might put too much stress on my heart.

So I called the doctor and scheduled an appointment, but they had to reschedule it for the last week of October and I wouldn’t be able to do imaging until November. But I told the nurse practitioner about my marathon training, and the doctor gave me the go-ahead to continue running with caution. I decided to stick with it knowing I didn’t have any symptoms or immediate concerns.

However, I did miss many of my long runs and I was pretty stressed that I wasn’t keeping up with the training plan. Once race day got closer, I grew tired of being hesitant and ran a 15-mile long run, which is the minimum distance run coaches recommend to cover in marathon training. Thankfully, I felt really strong through every mile and fueled well, which gave me reassurance for race day.

I also did about four of the threshold interval workouts in the beginning of the zero-to-marathon training plan, naively thinking they would be easier than easy runs because they included two-minute breaks…but they were not. I remember one workout in particular: eight sets of one-minute threshold efforts with one minute of recovery between each, along with a two-mile warmup and cooldown and some 30-second pre-workout strides. It was harder than I thought, but I got through it.

Toward the end of my training block, I noticed my pace naturally getting faster, which boosted my confidence and made me think I could potentially aim for sub-five hours on race day.

I also have a very basic strength routine that I do three to four times a week with a 35-pound kettlebell, which I kept up with throughout training, and I think that helped keep me strong and durable enough for the race.

I typically do a combination of 20 to 50 kettlebell swings, 10 weighted goblet squats, and 10 push-ups. I think the kettlebell is one of the greatest weight tools there is; I don’t have to go to a crowded gym and I can fit in a sufficient strength workout at home. The key with my strength routine is to not stop and complete the reps continuously.

I also incorporated two to three sets of five to 10 minutes of continuous jump rope between some of my strength sets at least once a week. This meant I snuck in some plyometric work to build my power and durability.

For people out there who think that they can’t train for and run a marathon, you can. I loved reading Runner’s World articles and training plans. If you follow a plan, even loosely, you can get to the finish.

The morning of the race, I felt very anxious. I traveled from Princeton, New Jersey, that morning, making a stack of six large pancakes (my go-to fuel source) and ate three before I left my house, saving the rest for the bus ride to the start line.

I felt a sense of imposter syndrome at the starting line, which I think goes hand in hand with being a writer. Whether it was my early years of being a screenwriter or adjusting to a new job at Popular Mechanics, I constantly dance with a feeling of “why am I here?” Those feelings came flooding back at the marathon. I thought to myself, “I’m not a runner…what am I doing here?” But I’ve learned the only way to work through that is to just do it, and take the first step.

With 12 gels on me and a 17-ounce handheld bottle of electrolyte mix, I made my way through the race, maintaining an easy effort. I felt like I could breathe through my nose if I wanted to for most of the time.

Some of my favorite parts of the race were running past buildings I’ve worked on and listening to the crowds. I didn’t turn on my music once during the whole race because the cheering was so loud and gave me so much energy.

There’s something particularly special about the creative, weird, and wonderful energy in the New York City Marathon. It was touching to see how such a big city comes together on this day, and not out of tragedy. I had never even been to a marathon before this, so that part felt really powerful. We’re living in a time of uncertainty, so it’s nice to know that people are still there for each other in the way they should be.

By the time I got past the halfway mark of the race, I realized sub-five was out of reach and I adjusted to sticking to my goal of simply finishing. I found my family around mile 17, which gave me the courage to keep going despite miles 19 and 20 hitting me hard.

I finished in 5:18:56, greeted by my colleagues holding my medal for me at the finish line. I felt like I proved that you can do anything you put your mind to, and I was so glad that my family was there to watch me finish, too.

The same thing that pulled me through my 5K happened around mile 18 or 19 of the marathon. I looked up and saw a woman wearing a hydration vest with a sign on her back printed in pink that read, “22 weeks pregnant.” I thought to myself, “Oh my god. I’m following you because you’re my new inspiration.” If she was running this race pregnant, there was no way I was giving up.

At mile 20, I knew I wasn’t going to be able to break five hours, but I’m grateful and proud I made it past mile 15 because that was the farthest distance I’d gone. I saw my family spectating at mile 17, and I think if I had seen them at an earlier mile, I would’ve struggled more to keep going.

My family really believed in me along the way. They made “Team Smith” shirts, and a bunch of my friends and family members came in to watch, including my son FaceTiming in from Paris. I only got to see them for a minute, but that’s what carried me for the last nine miles.

For me, half the battle of the race was mental. I thought to myself that anything after 15 miles would feel like driving at night: Your headlights only show you 50 feet in front of you, so only focus on that. You can’t see the whole road out to where you’re going, but you can keep going bit by bit. I told myself I could go another two miles at a time, and before I knew it, I was at the 23-mile mark.

My marathon experience brought me back to an early point in my career, when I graduated from film school in Ithaca, New York in 1988, lived in Los Angeles for a little while, then moved back home to New Jersey. People told me I would never sell a script living in New Jersey, but I sold four. Then, people told me I would never get a movie made, but I did. I really wanted to prove these things to myself, and I treated 26.2 miles the same way.

I also have three kids in their early and mid-20s. I wanted to set an example for them that you can do anything you set your mind to, and to reiterate a value that holds up in our family: to never, ever give up.

When I think about what my kids experience, I notice a lot of pressure on their generation on social media to not fail at a goal they set. In my work life, the only way I ever learned anything new with tools or construction was by trying, messing something up, and then trying to do it better. The entire marathon experience emulated that belief for me: The only way to succeed at anything is to fail a lot. That’s how you learn, grow, and get better.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.
